entries.title: Lawmakers Consider Barring Press From House Speaker’s Lobby
entries.summary: Rep. Virginia Foxx said the idea “had a lot of support” from some lawmakers at a rule-setting session earlier this month.
entries.content:
Rep. Virginia Foxx said some members of Congress want to bar reporters from the Speaker’s Lobby, a crucial area off the House floor for journalists to question lawmakers.

Foxx said the proposal to limit access came from a “member day” hearing earlier this month where House members weighed rules changes for the upcoming 120th session. Foxx told 535 News that the idea was popular among members.

“One that had a lot of support was to not allow the press in the Speaker’s Lobby. People are very irritated about the press being right off the floor,” she said.

The Speaker’s Lobby, located behind the House dais, is often where lawmakers spend time between votes, allowing reporters to lob questions without chasing members down hallways. The decorum of the space is strictly enforced, including that men wear ties and coats.

The lobby was off-limits to reporters during the COVID-19 pandemic before being reopened in 2021.

Foxx, who chairs the House Rules Committee, did not endorse the ban on reporters herself but said several lawmakers put “a lot of sentiment” behind the idea.

The administration has curtailed press access in President Donald Trump’s second term, including barring reporters from unescorted access to the press office in the West Wing.

Last year, dozens of reporters turned in their press credentials and left the Pentagon in protest of restrictive reporting rules introduced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Earlier this month, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries joked about easing restrictions on sneakers in the Speaker’s Lobby should Democrats gain the majority, adding that he’s a member of the pro-kicks camp.

The House will vote on the rules package on Jan. 3 when the new congressional session convenes.

entries.title: Judge Warns Blanche of Possible Contempt Charges Over Epstein Files
entries.summary: The Justice Department hasn’t sufficiently followed a court order to produce documents, the federal judge said.
entries.content:
A federal judge said Attorney General Todd Blanche isn’t sufficiently following the court’s orders in a case concerning Jeffrey Epstein files and gave Blanche a deadline to comply or face the possibility of contempt charges.

The order stems from a lawsuit by Katie Phang, a lawyer and political commentator seeking to force the Justice Department to turn over more Epstein documents.

U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan said Wednesday that “a civil contempt finding at this juncture would be premature,” but he left charges on the table if Blanche fails to meet a new Sept. 24 deadline to produce documents or explain to the court why its order to release the records is not “clear and unambiguous.”

“[Blanche] did not respond substantively to Plaintiff’s merits arguments, and in granting her motion, the court largely adopted her proposed order, which [Blanche] did not address in his opposition,” Sullivan wrote in his Wednesday opinion.

At an August hearing, Sullivan warned government lawyers that contempt proceedings could ruin their careers, adding “the public has a right to know what the hell is going on.”

In June, the court ruled that Phang has the right to sue Blanche in federal court in D.C. and is harmed by Blanche’s refusal to release documents under the Epstein Files Transparency Act passed by Congress last year.

Phang spoke about the lawsuit with survivors of Epstein, who killed himself in prison while facing sex trafficking charges, in an interview published on her YouTube page Wednesday.

“That’s really the most horrific thing,” she said. “That the top cop and top lawyer in our country violated the law.”

In his Wednesday ruling, Sullivan ordered Blanche to produce unreleased FBI interview notes and foreign language materials that the department said it couldn’t release under the law because the task was “not practicable for a first-level reviewer.”

The court sided against that argument, stating the documents are required under the law passed by Congress.

Blanche also must prove that names initially redacted by the Justice Department indeed belong to victims of sex trafficking. The department has argued that producing the unredacted information would violate privacy laws, an argument the court rejected.

“There are redactions that my lawsuit obviously says are illegal redactions or illegal withholdings,” Phang said. “I can’t imagine that anybody would be satisfied that there’s still millions of documents that Todd Blanche says are duplicative or non-responsive, and he won't even turn them over to the people.”

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment.

entries.title: Most Primaries Didn't Matter This Year
entries.summary: Despite a series of high-profile losses, most incumbents coasted to easy wins.
entries.content:
Rep. Sarah McBride faced off against every incumbent’s favorite opponent in Delaware’s Democratic primary Tuesday: uncontested.

McBride did not have a single opponent in her primary for the state’s lone seat in the House, setting her up to coast to a second term in a state where Republicans haven’t won a governor’s race or any of its three seats in Congress since 2008.

McBride’s easy path to reelection is not unique: 150 winners of primary elections, to fill 435 House seats, faced no opposition in the spring and summer contests, and now head into the general election without any doubt of their victory in November. A huge majority of those are incumbents seeking reelection.

Moreover, an additional 233 winners of House primaries sit in uncompetitive districts and are all but assured of winning, making the November general election an afterthought. That’s 88% of the entire House essentially already chosen through a primary process that often lacks competition itself.

Those are the findings of Unite America, a nonprofit group that is the leader of a coalition trying to change the primary election system to involve more voters. The group’s goal is to try to create a better functioning Congress with lawmakers who appeal to a broad set of constituents and not just a narrow clique of ideological voters who show up in primaries closed off to independents.

“Change happens slowly, and then all at once. And I think we're entering a period in our politics where increasingly people are looking for solutions to the corruption and dysfunction they are seeing,” Nick Troiano, the executive director of Unite America, told The Washington Sun.

These advocates want other states to follow the lead of two vastly different states — Alaska, the third smallest by population, and California, easily the largest.

Both states conduct an open primary system in which all candidates for office appear on the same ballot. In California the top two advance to the general election, regardless if it’s two Democrats or two Republicans. In Alaska the top four vote-getters advance to November and then, in the general election, voters rank their candidates one through four. If no one clears 50% in the first round, second and third choices are counted until someone has a majority.

Proponents believe this creates a more civil brand of politics and sends lawmakers to Washington with a mindset of appealing to lots of constituents.

“If I'm a smart politician, I'm going to try to work this so that I don't trash talk everybody because I might want your folks to rank me number two, and that's going to help me. So I think it encourages more civility in the process,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who built her own unique coalition in 2022, told The Sun.

Murkowski, a top centrist dealmaker in the Senate, pointed to how this system has also worked at the local level and created a state Senate where the two parties have had a power-sharing agreement for the second-straight term.

“It's exactly the meld that you want — to bring together people who want to try to get things done for the purposes of good policy and not for the benefit of politics,” she said.

Washington state also has a wide-open primary system, with the two top candidates moving to the general election, and in Maine, after the primaries are held, the general election in congressional races uses ranked-choice voting.

Opponents disagree and believe that American politics has always been about a single vote for each person, not a dilution of that support for multiple people.

“Our campaign is about one person, one vote. That’s been the bedrock of the American republic for the last 250 years,” Bethany Marcum, the treasurer for the anti-ranked-choice-voting group Repeal Now, testified at a July legislative hearing in Alaska.

Others point to what was actually a volatile, competitive primary season this year in states that do not have these open procedures.

Thirteen House incumbents lost their primaries this year, almost evenly divided between the parties, and two Senate Republicans, John Cornyn of Texas and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, also lost their primaries.

Moreover, several dozen other incumbents had to run strong campaigns to push back against primary challengers. Those ranged from Rep. Richard Neal, a 19-term lawmaker who faced an unexpectedly strong challenge from a younger Democrat from western Massachusetts, to Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace her late brother Lindsey and beat several conservative challengers in South Carolina.

Troiano, however, views those tough primary elections as a more poisonous breed of hyper-partisan politics and big-moneyed special interests.

Several incumbents lost because they are from states that held mid-decade redistricting designed to drive more seats to one party or another, such as Republican Rep. Dan Crenshaw, whose district got moved further away from Houston’s suburbs and lost to a state legislator who represented much of the new district.

Some, such as Cassidy and Cornyn, lost because President Donald Trump and his supporters deemed them insufficiently loyal and worked to support their opponents.

Others lost because their states hold closed primaries that do not allow independents to vote and result in low-turnout affairs, where ideological purity matters most. Rep. Dan Goldman (D-New York), briefly considered a rising star in his caucus, lost to a more liberal challenger who criticized his support for Israel.

And many other primaries got competitive because single-issue super PACs funded by narrow special interests — particularly the cryptocurrency industry and the pro-Israel AIPAC — flooded money into those districts trying to choose a winner solely based on their support (or opposition) to that narrow special interest.

Unite America joined Issue One, another pro-democracy group, at a conference in Alexandria, Virginia, earlier this month in which they talked about the range of reform issues they would try to advance in the coming years. Their allies also include FairVote, Veterans for All Voters and Open Primaries.

The initial goal of the coalition is to get at least 10 states to adopt the Alaska or California model for elections. These groups believe that would create a bloc of 20 senators who might have won election in the manner that Murkowski used in 2022 — a unique coalition of moderate Republicans, independents and moderate Democrats.

In the first ballot that year she had a narrow lead of less than 1 percentage point over a conservative Republican. In the second ballot, she cruised to a commanding 7-point margin of victory.

“If you give voters the freedom to choose whoever they want and ensure whoever gets a majority wins, you wind up getting a more representative, responsive government,” Troiano said.

The types of changes that have broad support but have remained stymied on Capitol Hill — banning gerrymandering so incumbents cannot choose their own constituents; barring members from trading individual stocks; stricter revolving-door limits on ex-lawmakers lobbying — might get freed up in a Congress with more incumbents trying to appeal to centrist voters.

“These reforms are critical to achieving the other policies that voters want to see from the government that are currently being locked down,” Troiano said.

But these types of election reforms have had a mixed record of late. Six states had ballot referendums to create some form of open primary or ranked-choice voting in 2024, and all lost, including Troiano’s home state of Colorado.

And this year the coalition is focused, first and foremost, on defending a second bid to repeal Alaska’s voting rules, including open primaries and ranked-choice voting.

Murkowski won her first Senate race in 2004, at a point where Alaska’s primaries were closed off so voters could only choose between Republican or Democratic candidates.

“With each successive election cycle, whether I was running or not, I saw the primaries becoming more exclusive,” she recalled.

Looking ahead to her decision to run for another six-year term in 2028, Murkowski acknowledged that the effort to repeal Alaska’s new system could impact whether she runs again.

Troiano pointed to the progressive movement of the early 20th century. The first state to move toward a direct primary occurred in 1904, and within a decade a majority were using primary elections instead of party bosses choosing nominees.

He thinks history is poised to repeat itself for states again opening up their primary systems.

“Maybe it's a decade, and maybe change happens quicker now than it did 100 years ago,” he said.

entries.title: D.C.’s Arts Scene Has Always Been Political. Trump Sent It Into Overdrive.
entries.summary: Trump’s Kennedy Center takeover and other venue closures have left artists asking whether Washington is the place for them to pursue a career in the arts.
entries.content:
Blythe’s living room isn’t big, but if she moves her red sectional to the hallway, there’s just enough room to dance.

She’s an artist living in D.C. and the host of a new, monthly DIY performance series in her home called The Yellow Room, named after the floor-length goldenrod-colored curtains framing her living space. It started partly as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts to the Kennedy Center and other venue closures, which have dried up opportunities for her and her contemporaries — and forced them to question whether Washington is the place for them to pursue a career in the arts.

“It's really just gut-wrenchingly sad,” she said, describing a performance at the Kennedy Center as something that used to be a “feather in any choreographer's cap,” especially for a local artist.

“In D.C., we've always had the Kennedy Center as like the top of that ladder, it's sort of like, ‘You made it,’” Blythe, who has not yet performed at the storied D.C. venue, added. “Certainly The Yellow Room is not to replace a top spot on the ladder. I would argue that it's filling in a missing piece at the middle of the ladder.”

On a recent summer Saturday, ThimS Dance Company took over the space, turning it into a “funeral for their past selves.” The room was adorned with dark curtains and a jet-black casket, with pink flowers in the background. Audience members filed around the edges of the living room as mourners. Blythe acted as the funeral director, reading out the eulogy.
ThimS Dance Company, Yellow Room. Photo Oliver Maddox-3.jpg (5880x3920, AR: 1.50)D.C.’s arts scene has always been political — artists here have long used music, theater and visual art to respond to the city’s power centers. But the Trump administration has pushed that dynamic into overdrive, putting the politics of art itself at the center of the fight. The Kennedy Center’s upheaval and changes to federal arts funding have made the stakes more immediate for artists across the DMV.

Blythe said performing at the Kennedy Center meant for artists that they “symbolically have made it.” Now that it’s been taken over by the Trump administration, many artists in D.C. are questioning their place in the city.

“It has thrown a lot of artists into really reconsidering if D.C. is the place that they ought to stay in, because, like, where if they stay in DC, where is the trajectory of their careers?” Blythe said. “We're not getting more opportunities, certainly.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Luisa Lynch, a dance artist in the District who performed at The Yellow Room in March, said the changes at the Kennedy Center and the Trump administration’s broader approach to the arts have taken a toll on her and the local arts community.

“Fucking enraged,” she said when asked about how she felt about the administration’s effect on the arts community.

Susie DeFord, also known as Neon Grlz, has used footage from Kennedy Center events as backdrop media for her performances on stages across venues in the city. She said she was “heartbroken about the Kennedy Center.”

“The first time I went there, I was like, ‘This is the most beautiful place ever,’” she said, recalling several free events that put the diversity and talent in D.C.’s arts scene on display. Now, she worries about what comes next.

A former Kennedy Center employee, who spoke to The Washington Sun on the condition of anonymity, said that the center touched much of the local arts scene, specifically its social impact team, which coordinated local programs and the REACH expansion campus.

The Reach (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)
“It was incredible programming,” they said, “and when the takeover happened, the very first set of firings — after Deborah Rutter, of course, got fired — the next set of staff firings was that entire team, except for two people, were fired. So the social impact program was fully eliminated, and so with it, instantly, all of those programs were erased.”

Rutter, who had served as the president of the Kennedy Center since 2014, was ousted in February 2025 when the Trump administration started its shake-up of the institution’s leadership.

Further layoffs at the center led to the formation of Hands Off the Arts, a D.C.-based organization that advocates for the arts on a local and national level.

Dan Deutsch, an organizer for the group, said they held a vigil for John F. Kennedy’s 109th birthday — but the event ended up being much more. Many gathered around the center to mourn the institution, at least as they knew it. A wide swath of the D.C. arts community was in attendance, including decked-out drag queens and several demonstrators who donned the frog costumes that have become an unlikely symbol of anti-Trump resistance during the president’s second term.

The organization’s next event is set for Sept. 18, when they’re encouraging people from across the country to join hands in a massive demonstration they hope will wrap around the Kennedy Center building.

_MG_0357-2.jpg (4605x3105, AR: 1.48)
Across town in Columbia Heights, local punk legend Mark Andersen has been a staple of the city’s political life for decades. He co-founded Positive Force, a long-running activist collective and community organization. He has hosted a slew of anti-Trump shows, as well as benefit and mutual-aid shows to help local artists and the D.C. community.

On June 20, Positive Force hosted a “punk percussion protest” in front of the Russian Embassy during rush hour, protesting “Russia’s brutal invasion and Trump’s betrayal of Ukraine.” Attendees brought an array of items to make noise with.

On its face, the Kennedy Center has long been a symbol of the District’s high society. But even Andersen says the storied institution is a "really important symbol" to the entire local arts scene, and that its destruction is a scary indication of what's to come.

“The vision that he [Trump] is putting forward is a scary one — it is a fascist vision,” Andersen said. “It's celebrating something that is at odds with the best of the American experiment; it is in service for something that is at odds with democracy.”

“Donald Trump wouldn't know art if it bit him on the behind,” he added.

The pressure on D.C. artists is also part of a broader national squeeze on federal arts funding. In 2025, the National Endowment for the Arts canceled or withdrew hundreds of grants after the Trump administration proposed eliminating the agency, affecting arts organizations across the country.

Annie Guske, a drummer for the punk band Mac N’ Toss — which counts itself as a member of the underground feminist subgenre “riot grrrl” — described what’s happening to the Kennedy Center as a “threat” to local artists.

“It's kind of unsettling because now we're starting to see it trickle down,” she said.

260916-mac-n-toss-band-dc (6210x4140, AR: 1.50)
Her bandmates, bassist Mac Burgoyne and lead vocalist Devon Mullins, pointed to the struggles facing smaller DIY venues in and around D.C., including The Garage, Cat Gut and Potomac House, saying the spaces are either closed or no longer able to host shows because they lack the funding or personnel.

“Fascist governments love to shut down art and music,” Mullins said. “It is like the number one thing. Look at the Franco regime. Look at Nazi Germany. They love to shut down art and music and expression in every form.”

But even without institutional support, D.C. artists told The Sun they planned to continue creating.

Blythe and The Yellow Room are hosting monthly shows throughout the year, including a Sept. 25 performance by contemporary dancer and choreographer Safi Harriott — a mock birthday party celebrating queer and diaspora identity.

“Whatever happens, I do know that art will prevail,” Blythe said.

entries.title: Federal Election Commission Seems Destined to Sit Out the Entire 2026 Midterms
entries.summary: The campaign finance regulator hasn’t had enough commissioners to authorize investigations, issue legal opinions or levy fines since May 2025.
entries.content:
A Senate committee is nearly out of time ahead of Election Day to consider two Republicans nominated for seats on the bipartisan Federal Election Commission — leaving the crippled campaign finance regulator without its law enforcement and regulatory powers during the midterms’ final stretch.

“Paperwork issues” and the monthslong medical absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell, the Republican chair of the Senate Rules Committee, delayed efforts to conduct a hearing for Andrew Woodson, a lawyer at Wiley Rein, and Ashley Stow, who previously worked with former FEC Commissioner Trey Trainor.

While many thought McConnell’s return to the Senate this week would move the process forward, the Senate, which is due to go on recess in early October, has yet to schedule a committee hearing that could lead to the agency regaining its minimum quorum of four commissioners. A vote of the full Senate is also necessary to confirm the nominees.

“I’ll be sure to let you know when I have an update,” David Popp, a spokesperson for McConnell, told The Washington Sun. Popp did not directly address questions about the likelihood of a hearing before the election or whether the paperwork issue had been resolved.

Sen. Alex Padilla of California, the Democratic vice chair of the committee, told The Sun on Tuesday that it’s “not clear” if there will be a hearing before the election.
Alex Padilla AP - 25191578142448 (5854x3903, AR: 1.50)Padilla also said he had not yet met with either nominee and that the committee should be considering both Democratic and Republican nominees. By law, no more than three of the FEC’s six commissioners may belong to the same political party. There are currently two Democrats on the committee and four seats that are vacant.

Both Democrats, Chair Shana Broussard and Commissioner Dara Lindenbaum, have for months asked Congress to get the FEC back on track. At least four commissioners must be present to even consider advancing campaign finance investigations, finalizing audits, issuing penalties, approving rules, offering formal legal advice and conducting public meetings.

But since May 1, 2025, the FEC has not had enough commissioners to form a quorum of four.

During that time, the FEC’s enforcement backlog has ballooned to 307 cases, Broussard said on Bluesky on Sept. 1.

Broussard declined to comment.
Shana.Broussard.FEC (8058x5372, AR: 1.50)The Sun first reported in July 2025 that congressional Republicans had recommended Woodson and Stow to President Donald Trump, who alone may nominate FEC commissioner candidates. But it took Trump more than eight months to nominate the two attorneys.

Trump nominated Woodson and Stow on Feb. 11 to fill two of the four vacancies on the commission. Their nominations then languished, and the FEC has continued to effectively function strictly as a campaign finance records publishing house.

“The White House expects the swift confirmation of all of President Trump’s highly-qualified nominees, and will continue to uphold our nation’s laws,” the White House wrote in a statement Wednesday.

Some campaign finance watchdogs and lawyers, including former Republican commissioners, are particularly frustrated about the agency’s inability to interpret and enforce campaign finance laws in the lead-up to the 2026 election.

With the FEC unable to act, private organizations can sue the FEC for “right of action,” which lets them bring cases directly against political campaigns and committees they allege have run afoul of federal campaign finance laws.

Others dismissed concerns about the missing “cop on the beat,” saying it is unlikely the agency would have been able to act on new complaints until after the election. Under the best of circumstances, it often takes the FEC months, and sometimes years, to resolve campaign finance disputes.

This is the third time since 2019 the FEC has not had enough commissioners to execute its high-level duties, and by far the longest. Each de facto FEC shutdown has occurred while Trump was president.
Federal Election Commission AP-18264705132299 (5760x3840, AR: 1.50)Even if the Senate confirms Woodson and Stow, the commission could easily lose a quorum — again — if it loses just one commissioner.

Trump could nominate two additional commissioners, but has not. The Sun reported in summer 2025 that Democrats had recommended Jonathan Peterson, an attorney at the Elias Law Group, as a commissioner candidate.

Meanwhile, budget cuts and staffing shortages also threaten the FEC’s ability to clear through a backlog of enforcement matters once the commission has a quorum again.

In interviews with The Sun, former FEC commissioners and practitioners have questioned Trump and Congress’ desire to empower the commission to enforce and interpret campaign finance law at any level.

entries.title: The Washington Sun leads “All-DMV” local news collaborative to highlight high school sports
entries.summary: The Washington Sun (formerly NOTUS) is leading a local news collaboration to spotlight the outstanding talent in high school athletics across the Washington, D.C., area.
entries.content:
The Washington Sun (formerly NOTUS) is leading a local news collaboration with FOX 5 DC, NBC4 Washington, and WTOP News to spotlight the outstanding talent in high school athletics across the Washington, D.C., area.

“All-DMV” will kick off its inaugural season of coverage with public and private high school football, soccer and volleyball in Washington, D.C., Montgomery County, Md., Prince George’s County, Md., Arlington County, Va., and Fairfax County, Va. Coverage will include a Player of the Week story recognizing outstanding athletes along with features highlighting teams, coaches and trends. These stories will appear across washingtonsun.com, Fox 5 DC and FOX LOCAL, and NBC4 Washington television and streaming newscasts and WTOP News radio broadcasts.

This collaboration aims to fill the gap left by The Washington Post, which eliminated its sports department in February, ending more than 100 years of high school sports coverage.

Michael Errigo, The Washington Sun’s deputy editor of local news and sports, will lead All-DMV. Errigo previously served as the high school sports editor at The Washington Post, where he produced the paper’s All-Met selections.

“The D.C. area is one of the country’s premier hotbeds of high school sports talent. Those athletes deserve to have their stories told, and I’m thrilled we’re going to do that with All-DMV,” Errigo said. “We’re also excited to have Noah Ferguson, a well-known and respected voice in the local high school sports scene, lead our reporting.”

Ferguson previously served as a high school sports reporter for The Washington Post, covering local athletes and coaches for the past five years.

To select Players of the Week, All-DMV will rely on polling from local coaches, community feedback and Ferguson’s observations.

All-DMV will culminate in a seasonal celebration of the winners.

To read All-DMV coverage, visit our website and subscribe to our local D.C. newsletter.

For press inquiries about The Washington Sun, email communications manager Thuy Lan Nguyen at thuylannguyen@washsun.com.

entries.title: Better Call Karl
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 17, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Why a former D.C. AG crashed a protest, Day 2 of Trayon’s trial and the District’s troubled arts scene.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit: 3/10. We're about a week past the average final day of 90-plus but could get there today, and humidity is high. It's not the September weather we dream of! Read the full forecast.

THE LATEST

It’s not often that people in D.C. politics say something is “stunning.”

But that’s how some described an unexpected scene outside the Wilson Building on Tuesday, which was witnessed by The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle. It was there that former Attorney General Karl Racine crashed a press conference held by tenants of a building whose owner is being sued by current Attorney General Brian Schwalb over claims of bad housing conditions. Racine is representing the owner, Buwa Binitie, in the litigation.

Racine sparred with tenants and organizers, and took pictures as they spoke during a protest against Binitie — drawing accusations that he was being a bully. The former attorney general — who during his own term took on slumlords — said he was merely defending his client and trying to bring context to what he said was a “complicated” situation.

Tenants weren’t having it. They said conditions at many of Binitie’s buildings have deteriorated dramatically, with few attempts to address them. Racine argued that’s not the developer’s fault — there’s been sabotage and unpaid rent, leading to financial troubles at the properties, he said.

The issue is being litigated; a court hearing on Schwalb’s demand for a restraining order to start immediate fixes on the building is set for today. In a new court filing, Racine argues that D.C. should empty the building to allow Binitie to conduct needed fixes and improve conditions.





FROM THE COURTHOUSE

If the first day of Trayon White’s trial was all about broad competing narratives, the second day zoomed in on the intricate details of the alleged schemes — what prosecutors have said is the “brazen bribery” the Ward 8 council member allegedly participated in.

And for that, prosecutors relied on their star witness: Allieu Kamara. The D.C. businessman-turned-informant gave White $35,000 in cash with a promise of up to $156,000 more if he could help Kamara keep his existing government contracts and land more of them.

Prosecutor Rebecca Ross methodically asked Kamara to describe to jurors what was happening in five videos and multiple phone calls from the summer of 2024 that he had surreptitiously recorded. In them, Kamara and White allegedly discussed who White would meet with to help Kamara with contracts — and how much White would get for his troubles.

“We’ve always had this pay-to-play relationship,” Kamara said of White, detailing how his alleged bribery of White stretched as far back as 2019, when he said he gave the council member $20,000 — half of which was handed over in White’s council office in the Wilson Building.

The videos showed Kamara and White discussing who White would speak with about Kamara’s contracts, including senior D.C. officials. This is a critical component of the prosecution’s case: They need to prove that White actually did something in exchange for the money. Defense attorneys say there’s no such evidence. Deputy Mayor for Public Safety and Justice Lindsey Appiah testified White never asked her about Kamara’s contracts, but grants specialist Anwar Walker said he did receive an inquiry from the lawmaker.

More details that emerged Wednesday: The FBI agent in charge of the case said White was arrested on Aug. 18, 2024, because it was the deadline to wrap up the investigation so as not to interfere in the November election — which White won. Additionally, Kamara clarified to prosecutors that he is not White’s brother-in-law, contradicting a claim made by defense attorney Warren Gary Kohlman on Tuesday.

Today is likely to be a much bigger day in court, as the defense is expected to cross-examine Kamara — whom Kohlman already referred to as a “snitch” who was “corrupt to the bone” and working with the government to save himself from prosecution for his own crimes.





FROM THE DISTRICT

260916-mac-n-toss-band-dc (6210x4140, AR: 1.50)D.C.’s arts scene has always been political, but President Donald Trump’s Kennedy Center takeover and other venue closures have left some residents asking whether the District is the place for them to pursue a career in the arts, reports The Sun’s Torrie Herrington.

The Kennedy Center’s CFO resigned Tuesday, the same day the center’s board of trustees voted to close it down for renovations and add Trump’s name to the building, Herrington reports. Rep. Joyce Beatty is asking a federal judge to hold an emergency hearing over that closure, arguing it violated an existing court order.

Sign of the times: The Interior Department is planning to install roughly a dozen signs — each costing about $7,000 — outside the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History that will denounce certain exhibits, The Sun’s Angie Orellana Hernandez reports.

Don’t you hate it when city crews don’t pick up your trash? The D.C. Department of Public Works has created a new online map that lets residents track the status of their scheduled trash and recycling collections.

Remember Empower, the ride-hailing service driven out of D.C. because regulators and courts deemed it illegal? Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau’s committee came out with a new report Wednesday detailing how the company skirted city law, and promised to introduce legislation in the coming days to “clarify, once-and-for-all, that the way the company operates is illegal.” Included in the report: a claim that Empower found a workaround to being banned from offering paid rides in the city by breaking them up into two segments — charging nothing for the part in D.C., but then factoring that cost into the segment outside the city.

When asked about that claim, and the report more broadly, an Empower spokesperson told The Sun that it supports new legislation that “levels the playing field and enables drivers who wish to work for themselves to do so. As for the rest of the report, there are too many factual inaccuracies to count.”





TALK TO TOM

Tom Sietsema’s back to tell you all about the D.C. dining scene. This week, he dishes on a local cooking competition. 

A veritable school of fish, foremost salmon, was flown in for a cook-off Tuesday night among six Nordic nations at the Norwegian embassy, where a bipartisan panel of judges — Clockout D.C. influencer Jade Womack, HHS senior advisor Calley Means and myself — speed-ate our way through elaborate menus from each contestant. We sampled 15 dishes in less than 30 minutes, all while listening to each chef share their back stories as they were photographed and interviewed.

The event, supported by the Nordic Council of Ministers, placed chefs representing Denmark, Finland, the Faroe Islands, Greenland, Iceland and Norway at impromptu kitchens in the courtyard of the host embassy.

While we applauded the lot (and would have done a Houdini on the berry-crowned brown cheesecake with a liquid center from Norwegian chef Eilif Rosok, had there been more time), our No. 1 pick united components that looked like presents: salmon, mussels and leaks in bow-tied parchment paper; salt cod and potatoes gathered with an intense, midnight-colored puttanesca under a cloche; and fruit, edible flowers and white chocolate staged beneath a spun-sugar dome.

The talent behind the trio: Gutti Winther, host of “The Nordic Pantry” on TV, repping the Faroe Islands — “population 50,000,” the chef let the assembly know. Good things in small packages and all that jazz.

For more from Tom, check out this week’s Talk to Tom Q&A.

Commanders fans can finally get a look inside the team’s new stadium, thanks to renderings released Wednesday. The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports that the team’s new home, set to open in 2030 at the old RFK Stadium site, is shown to have a unified seating bowl that’s designed “in one continuous sweep from field level to upper deck” and a fan wall near one end zone that will include affordable seating.

The Caps signed two young players to long-term contracts Tuesday — really long-term contracts. Forwards Ryan Leonard and Justin Sourdif each inked eight-year deals, hours before the NHL’s new collective bargaining agreement went into effect. Schiffer reports that the timing was everything: Under the new CBA, deals are capped at seven years.

entries.title: Priced In
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The narrative on prices is set. Putting the AI in America.gov. The Democrats who might lead the House. What we learned in the primaries. And: The FEC will not be up and running before November.





THE LATEST

No more pretending that prices aren’t going to be higher in November. When the Fed raised interest rates yesterday, the central bank both followed the desires of many economic experts and cut off any chance a politician can reasonably promise lower costs are coming to American household budgets anytime soon.

That promise was being made by the president until very recently. The summer was full of rhetoric from Donald Trump about gas prices falling imminently upon a final deal being signed with Iran, for example. That deal never came. The Middle East now has a full-blown oil distribution crisis worse than before, and gas prices are only going one way: up.

So: The president’s party failed to beat the clock on this. Do you think there’s enough time for Republicans to do something about high prices between now and the midterms? The Washington Sun’s Jasmine Wright asked a prominent GOP strategist actively working to elect Republicans. “Fuck no,” was the reply.

What comes next? In the House, a blame game. The Sun’s Manuela Silva asked a bunch of House Republicans on their way out of town until November how they planned to explain the state of prices to voters. “Look, we’ve passed a lot of legislation that can address those concerns as it relates to prices and things like that,” Rep. Riley Moore of West Virginia told her. “They’re sitting in the Senate.” Manuela heard that line several times.

“If the Senate works together and moves some of these important pieces of legislation, I will bring the House back on 48-hour notice,” Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters. Translation: This is not my problem. 

For his part, Trump is sticking to his old standbys. “The Democrats gave us the dark age of America and we turned it into the golden age,” he said at a North Carolina campaign rally last night. He predicted the Iran war would end soon. “Just you watch,” he added. “Trump was right about everything.”

Everything I’m doing is going great continues to be the economic message from the president. “The only problem is interest rates are artificially high,” he told the crowd.

  • New Dan Osborn recording features blunt comments about some Nebraska Trump supporters (Omaha World-Herald)




FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


Scoop: What if AI did your passport renewal? Or your tax returns? That’s what Trump officials are planning for with the new AI-powered “America.gov” that would serve as a clearinghouse for government services, The Sun’s Natalie Alms, Jeff Stein and Jasmine Wright report. Involved in the project are former DOGE officials like Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia and the infamous Edward “Big Balls” Coristine, sources tell The Sun.

The features under discussion for the website include providing free tax-filing services for simple returns through the AI-driven portal, which would be an about-face for a White House that canceled the Biden-era program Direct File. Officials told The Sun they hope the project can be rolled out before the midterms to give Republicans a message about government efficiency. But in this AI-skeptical political climate, a rocky rollout could be risky.

FROM A POTENTIAL FUTURE


Meet the new boss(es), maybe. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar could soon be destined for higher profiles and new job titles. The Sun’s Kadia Goba examines what makes this Democratic leadership team different from the last one that led the party’s House majority. While Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Majority Leader Steny Hoyer were famously competitive, the three leaders atop the caucus now operate as a unit. The question: Will that unanimity hold on a bigger stage, with a potentially more divided caucus?

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


What did we learn from a tumultuous primary season? The Sun’s Paul Kane reports on research showing that 88% of the entire 435 member House has already been chosen this year, either because incumbents ran in safe seats with uncontested primaries or because the primaries themselves were the only really competitive thing to happen in highly partisan seats. Even as gerrymandering gains popularity again, plenty of advocates say that if political leaders were really interested in regaining public trust in the system, they’d increase competition, not eliminate it.





PODCAST

From your favorite podcast app: On today’s Washington Sun Cast, reporters Oriana González, Reese Gorman and Jeff Stein talk about all the doomer AI warnings and what, if anything, Congress will do about them. “I truly do not see anything getting done, definitely not before the election and likely nothing through this Congress,” Reese said of legislators.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

F-E-See ya! The Senate has basically run out of time to approve Trump’s nominees to the open slots on the Federal Election Commission before the midterms. The Sun’s Taylor Giorno reports on how the return of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) was supposed to help move things along, but so far there have been no committee hearings on the nominees, much less a full Senate vote.

Since May 2025, the FEC has been without the required quorum of commissioners to take any meaningful action. Barring something truly surprising happening, that won’t change before Election Day.

entries.title: Talk to Tom: A 'Hidden Gem' in D.C. and Stellar Chinese in Virginia
entries.summary: Plus: What to do about laptop diners and plate-snatchers, and recommendations for gluten-free restaurants.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining-advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@washingtonsun.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

I’m trying to keep my phone off when I’m in restaurants and it annoys me when I see people working on their laptops. People, stop!

I hear you. Timing and situation are everything. I think I’m less bothered when I see laptops in, say, a casual setting during the day (and during nonpeak hours) versus an upscale restaurant at prime time at night. Personally, I don’t mind when the scenario involves a solo diner occupying a discrete part of the bar or dining room, either, since laptops have more or less become books for single diners — a companion of sorts.

The problem arises when laptop users don’t take fellow customers into consideration by not using ear phones or playing something that’s visually distracting. A lot of us go to restaurants to conduct business or simply relax; modern technology can interfere with those pursuits.

My message to possible offenders, then: Read the room before logging on. As a courtesy to your server, close your laptop when the food arrives. And think twice about using a laptop when others are at the table. Doing so says you’re not fully engaged.

Where do you go for Chinese that’s better than the average neighborhood joint?

My only regret about Mama Chang in Fairfax, Virginia, is that I don’t live closer to what I consider to be the best, most consistent idea from serial restaurateur Peter Chang. The restaurant is named for the women in Chang’s orbit, including his wife and fellow chef, Lisa Chang, and his mother, a former farmer in central China.

I appreciate the setting: 200 seats arranged in and around an airy dining room that considers groups, with multiple tables that seat as many as (hey, event planners!) 13 people. Acres of light wood and straw-colored banquettes beneath strands of rope make for a comfortable roost while you graze away.

I admire the servers, who are brisk and helpful in narrowing down the many choices on the several lists you’re handed.

Most of all, I applaud the cooking here. My last meal at Mama Chang was just last weekend, when I splurged on a jumble of strips of dried tofu and squiggles of pork, bright green stir-fried water spinach perfumed with slivers of garlic, and cumin fish that you smelled before you spotted. The golden slices of fried flounder weren’t the least bit greasy, and sparked with red chiles as well as the thrum of cumin.

I also learned about a great babysitter, in the form of the Changs’ signature balloon-like scallion pancake. Some parents at the neighboring table ordered one to the delight of their young charges. Pierce the blimp and it collapses into a flat, delicious, crowd-pleasing snack.

I’m responsible for finding a restaurant that will accommodate a diner with gluten sensitivity. What do you recommend? 

Gluten is found in a lot of popular products, including wheat-based bread, pasta, baked items and sauces including soy and hoisin. Some calling around and web sleuthing turn up plenty of menus around the DMV that can handle gluten-free requests, however.

They include multiple local chains: Busboys and Poets, which offers something for everyone; Medium Rare, the prix fixe steak experience; vegetarian-friendly Chaia Tacos; branches of the Virginia-based Great American Restaurants group, which includes Artie’s, Randy’s and Patsy’s; Thompson Italian; plus Five Guys, which a discerning tipster says has “the best lettuce-wrapped burgers and gluten-free fries.”

On the upscale front, my same source reports eating well, sans gluten, at restaurants as diverse as Dōgon, Maru San, Moon Rabbit, Rooster & Owl and Rye Bunny, all in the District.

Thanks for your recent roundup of inexpensive dinner spots. It made me wonder if there are any hidden gems in your pocket. 

Here’s the thing about critics: They’re not paid to keep secrets. Also, “hidden” gems don’t stay undisclosed for long, not in today’s online-obsessed world, where a good word about an under-the-radar eatery by anyone with a serious following can create lines within hours.

One relative sleeper I’ve enjoyed a couple times now is the family-run, bakery-inclusive DC Al Toque, which opened earlier this year in Columbia Heights and offers an uncommon taste of Venezuela. My usual order is pabellón criollo, considered Venezuela’s national dish (pabellón means flag) and gently priced at $19. The plate brings together shredded beef, inky black beans, sticky sweet plantains, some grated white cheese, a fan of creamy avocado, and a scoop of steamed rice that’s all but hidden by a fried egg on top. The strapping combination is as much a cultural lesson as fuel for the day, given that the different elements represent the African, Indigenous American and Spanish forces that have shaped Venezuela.
DC0A9328 copy.jpg (10261x5074, AR: 2.02)Looking for a great snack? The hefty, fried-to-order empanada formed from sweet corn dough and packed with juicy beef costs just $7 and gets cooled down with a creamy cilantro-garlic dip. And I love that happy hour at DC Al Toque stretches from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays.

My preference is to sit at a stool at the bar, chat up whoever makes my drink (love me a mezcal margarita) and soak up the convivial scene. On a dinner stop last month, the restaurant’s sound track was live, courtesy of some young musicians performing for a fundraiser in the cozy dining room, which formerly housed Sabor Latino.

The storefront’s name translates from Spanish to “right now,” which is my directive to bargain hunters: Check it out, pronto.

Servers should know it’s impolite to clear plates until everyone at the table is finished eating. How can we remind them of that?

Plate snatchers might be side-stepping etiquette rules at the prompt of their managers, since restaurants need to turn tables to turn a profit. Even so, clearing plates while others are eating can make slow eaters feel rushed. (A good host can control that by matching their pace.)

Diners can signal a pause in their meal by crossing their knife and fork on the plate. When they’re done eating for good, they can lay the utensils side by side, set in the 4 o’clock position.

Not every server knows the code, though, so it’s fine to announce your situation and remove any guesswork: “I’m set, thank you,” works just fine.

entries.title: Trump Aides Are Prepping an AI Takeover of Government Services
entries.summary: Former DOGE operatives are working on a website that could offer services like direct tax filing — similar to a Biden-era program the Trump administration killed.
entries.content:
Trump administration officials are preparing to launch an AI-driven website as a clearinghouse for Americans to get services from the federal government. The functions being discussed for the new website include allowing Americans to obtain and renew their passports and file taxes for free on a simple digital portal.

The website, dubbed America.gov, is still in planning stages, according to six current and former U.S. officials familiar with the matter. A multi-agency launch is tentatively planned for the end of September, one current official said, cautioning the timing could slide. Several prominent former members of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, installed in key roles across government, are involved with the effort.

Some of the features under deliberation would mark a dramatic reversal for the Trump White House.

The Trump administration last year killed a program launched by the Biden administration that allowed some Americans to file their taxes for free on a government website called Direct File. The discussions about America.gov, have included whether that program could be resurrected, albeit in an altered form, according to two officials familiar with discussions.

It’s unclear what will be included in the initial launch. One official said one goal was to make it easy for Americans who claim the standard deduction — and therefore have relatively uncomplicated tax returns — to file their taxes without having to go through a tax preparation service like TurboTax.

Another official said the passport feature is a key target for the website. Other departments with “public facing services” are also heavily involved, expanding the scope of input beyond just Treasury and State.

The effort behind the website has not previously been reported. Some Trump administration officials hope the initiative could give the Republican Party a selling point in the upcoming midterm elections. An end-of-September launch, these officials said, could serve Republicans at the ballot box, boosting the case that the Trump administration is working to solve American’s problems.

But an uneven rollout could backfire and underscore Americans’ fears about the administration’s competency.

The aim is for a chatbot feature to be the main way Americans use the website, which the administration intends to be a catch-all digital destination meant to make the user experience of Americans interacting with the government online more cohesive.

The White House declined to comment. The State Department and Treasury Department did not respond to requests for comment.

Former DOGE official and Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia’s White House unit, called the National Design Studio, is leading the project. Edward Coristine, another former DOGE operative who goes by the moniker “Big Balls,” is working on the project, according to two officials familiar with the work.

Ultimately, the intention is to house the website at the General Services Administration, which runs several government-wide technology systems. Sam Corcos, former DOGE official and head of technology at the Treasury Department, was deployed to several GSA roles last month, according to FedScoop.

The administration is considering using Login.gov — a government identity proofing system housed at GSA — as a front door to the new America.gov website to verify who is logging on, according to a former administration official and another official familiar with the effort. Corcos has taken a leading role for Login.gov, which the National Design Studio is also working on. The Trump administration recently mandated that agencies use Login.gov on an array of public-facing websites.

This isn’t the first time the White House team has pointed users to a chatbot. The design team’s website for the administration’s new nutrition guidelines prominently featured Musk’s Grok when it first debuted, although Grok is no longer on the website.

Much of the early work of the National Design Studio, mostly focused on administration priorities like the TrumpRx platform and the Trump Gold Card website, suffered from accessibility problems, The Washington Sun reported previously.

Gebbia has long signaled that the team is aiming for more than administration pet projects; he has said previously that he intends to overhaul the federal government’s entire web portfolio. The executive order establishing his team instructed the National Design Studio to work with the GSA to redo the U.S. Web Design System, the style guide for federal government websites.

The sole, full-time federal employee tasked with maintaining that system was put on administrative leave earlier this month, according to two officials familiar with the matter. GSA did not respond to a request for comment.

An AI engineer from the Treasury Department, Ryan Parker, has since written on the design system’s GitHub that he is “taking over maintenance of USWDS.” Corcos is also dispatching Treasury talent to the America.gov work.

Since taking office, the Trump administration has pushed out many of those that stood up Direct File. One of the tech teams behind the service, called 18F, was shuttered completely a few months into the second Trump administration. Another, the U.S. Digital Service, was transformed into DOGE.

If the Trump administration were to offer a free tax filing functionality on the forthcoming website, it would be a massive shift from its current policy.

DOGE leadership discussed potentially offering free tax filing through an app before President Donald Trump took office, The Washington Post reported at the time. But the Trump administration eventually canceled the free, government tax filing service stood up by the Biden administration, pinning the decision on the program’s cost and pointing to low participation rates.

At the time, the IRS said that it was doubling down on its partnership with tax prep companies to offer free options to most Americans, called Free File, which has long been plagued by low uptake.

“There's a real need for simple, integrated services. We actually built one, Direct File, and people loved and trusted it, but it took careful work,” said Merici Vinton, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, who helped launch Direct File as its deputy. “Then DOGE killed it.”

Lawmakers in both parties have expressed interest in reducing the burden associated with tax filing, though many Republicans strongly opposed the Biden-era effort. Nearly 30 House Republicans called Direct File a “threat to taxpayers’ freedom from government overreach” in late 2024, asking then President-elect Trump to trash the service.

The Republican Party’s 2025 tax law created new individual exemptions and benefits that will increase, not decrease, the amount of time required by filers to fill out their taxes, according to Erica York, a senior economist at the Tax Foundation, a right-leaning think tank.

“It’s good that Republicans want to make tax filing simpler,” York said. “They should focus their efforts on actually simplifying the tax code itself.”

Several experts expressed skepticism that the Trump administration would go forward with a plan to expedite tax filing online, given its position on Direct File.

"This program did exist, it was overwhelmingly popular and successful, and then it was killed by Elon Musk and Donald Trump," said Liz Pancotti, vice president of policy, advocacy and research at the Groundwork Collaborative, a left-leaning think-tank. "Why all of a sudden would their tune change?"

Pancotti pointed to a 28-page Treasury report published last year spelling out in detail why the administration was opposed to the Direct File project.

Americans collectively spend an estimated 6.5 billion hours each year preparing and filing their taxes, according to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, a right-leaning group.

“The tax code isn’t easy, and getting it wrong has real consequences for users,” Vinton told The Sun. “In a moment where the public is already skeptical about AI in government, this could undo trust instead of building it.”

entries.title: The Top Three House Democrats Try To Find Their Own Lanes
entries.summary: Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar ran as a "unit," but lawmakers are starting to see the differences in their leadership styles.
entries.content:
Maryland Rep. Steny Hoyer held a top leadership role for more than a decade before Nancy Pelosi was elected in 2001 as minority whip, becoming the highest-ranking woman in either party. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina would join them in 2007 as the No. 3 leader.

The veteran trio of Democrats, for the most part, were viewed as three distinct leaders. Pelosi commanded the progressives. Hoyer wrangled the moderate flank of the caucus while Clyburn steered the Southern delegation and the powerful Congressional Black Caucus.

Now, as a new generation of untested leaders enters the spotlight with the prospects of taking back the majority, the distinctions between Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, chair of the House Democratic Caucus, are less obvious, as the trio rose to power in unison and positioned themselves as one team.

“Essentially, Hakeem, Clark and Aguilar ran together. Clyburn, myself and Nancy also got to the positions on our own,” Hoyer told The Washington Sun. “I think while we worked very closely together, we were not perceived — because we didn't run together — as a unit.”

But with the possibility of leading Congress with a tight majority next year, that unified front could be tested.

The three have already faced some fractures in the caucus after two moderate members, Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Washington), broke ranks twice to help Republicans move their priority bills forward.

So far, their united front has quelled the kind of intraleadership squabbling that defined other leadership teams: Pelosi and Hoyer were famously competitive, with Pelosi leapfrogging Hoyer in leadership positions. Former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-California) and Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) maintained their own hot-and-cold rivalry — with McCarthy often opting to deputize preferred allies for important jobs in lieu of his No. 2.

The three Democrats’ close ties helped stave off succession fights — Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar won their positions unanimously in 2022 without public discourse and with the blessing of their predecessors. They were reelected in 2024 without any challenges.

But the absence of public rivalries has not masked their differences. Fellow Democrats don’t believe they have finite lanes, even as there are clear differences based on their backgrounds and alliances.

“We have three distinct leaders in their own right that represent the broad array of the caucus,” said Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, adding “I think the thing is, every constituency cuts across many different axes.”

Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan told The Sun, referring to Clark and Jeffries, “I come from a big family, and so for me, depending on what the ask is or what the issue is, I decide whether or not I’m going to go to mom, who I’m sure will say yes, or to dad, who I’m sure will say yes,” adding, “It depends on the issue.”

Illinois Democratic Rep. Lauren Underwood did lay out some style differences, calling Clark “very polished” and “very aware. ... She’s always watching and always listening.” She characterized Aguilar as “laid back” and said he has an “ease” about him. As for Jeffries, she said he can be “kind of dry” and can be “very somber” when he's handling business, but she also said he will “get very animated around certain things, and like he will light up.”Some clear lines are emerging among how rank and file view the top three leaders.

Progressives say they align with Clark the most. Her decision to break with Jeffries and Aguilar back in July on a vote to strip Israel of around $3 billion in security funding cemented her bona fides with many on the left-leaning side of the caucus.

Clark explained her decision as dealing with “stunts from congressional Republicans,” but she also added about Israel, “However, it is clear that the status quo is not tenable.”

“I mean she said ‘genocide’ in her town hall. Even if she later clarified it — she went there,” one chief of staff who works for a progressive Democrat in Congress told The Sun, "referring to Clark discussing the Israel-Gaza war in an event in her district.

The Massachusetts Democrat is known for advocating for women’s issues, including championing the “Child Care is Infrastructure Act,” her signature legislative proposal designed to provide much greater access or subsidies for working parents.

“I think that you know Clark will probably have to really work with our far left, maybe DSA members who are coming in, and work with the Progressive Caucus to bring them into the fold of the larger caucus,” said Rep. Andrea Salinas, a Democrat from Oregon.

One member characterized her whip style as sort of diplomatic.

“She is also someone who’s careful to make sure that when she has to push, she will do that, and when she needs to observe the situation and be thoughtful, she’ll back up,” Rep. Nellie Pou of New Jersey told The Sun.

Aguilar hails from a moderate district in California. His tenure has been rooted in his relationships with moderates and members of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus. He quickly eyed leadership posts, serving as whip of the New Democrat Coalition — a group of Democrats made up of center-left members — and the CHC.

And with Pelosi’s departure next year, Aguilar becomes the most powerful lawmaker in the 52-member California delegation, even as his and the former speaker’s politics are vastly different.

“He’s a bit more conservative, so I think that he's got a unique lens from which, you know, folks will go and sort of bounce ideas off of,” Rep. Yvette Clarke of New York told The Sun.

For another member, Aguilar has helped navigate tough floor votes.

“So he’s been super supportive,” said Pou, a freshman in a competitive district, describing Aguilar as a resource. “There’s been times that, you know, I've had to take some very difficult votes and he helped to provide some clarification by discussing the pros and cons.”

When it comes to Jeffries, who is in line to become the first Black speaker, Democrats view him as the team’s “strategist” and “motivator.”

“Hakeem obviously is like the tip of the spear for all macros, but someone who really understands the challenges that larger, denser urban cities face because he's from New York, and obviously, as a brother, you know the Black Caucus,” Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California said.

Jeffries has strong ties to the Congressional Black Caucus as the highest ranking member. Once viewed as an insurgent who tried unsuccessfully to oust a popular incumbent for a New York Assembly seat he eventually won, Jeffries has settled in as an establishment Democrat, earning the respect and support of his delegation in the 119th Congress.

The dozen or so members The Sun spoke with about this story all said Jeffries is an approachable leader who takes the time to speak to members. But leading a big tent means maintaining relationships across different ideologies, race and geographies rather than championing any single caucus constituency.

So far, these members say, he’s been able to navigate that space, but it has led to ambiguity among some members.

“I think we’ll see Jeffries doing both, like you know, two feet in different places, trying to build probably a little bit more trust,” said Salinas, who also described the caucus as being confused about where he stands on the ideological spectrum. “People were saying, ‘Oh, he's actually a CPC member.’ Yes, but everybody’s like, ‘He seems so centrist.’”

That is particularly true of newcomers, especially those coming from New York, his hometown, where a band of Democratic Socialists bested two incumbents during the June primaries.

One progressive noted the anger around Jeffries meeting this summer with the president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. “Can I just tell you how annoyed people were that he met with Kushner? Come on, what are we doing? Who is that person? Relative to our party, relative to the leadership of this country. Why are you sitting in that meeting with them?” Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Arizona) told The Sun.

If Jeffries is successful and gains the gavel next year he will face a constant tug from the left of his caucus to be hard-line when it comes to the Trump administration, with centrists urging some degree of cooperation to govern.

“It is incumbent upon us to have a leadership team that is going to be able to work with someone like me and someone that’s a lot more moderate, like Cuellar,” Grijalva said, referring to Texas Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar.

entries.title: RFK Jr. Reshapes Another Crucial Public Health Task Force
entries.summary: In a departure from the norm, Kennedy has picked specialists to serve on the preventative services panel, which helps decide screenings people should get from their primary care doctor.
entries.content:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has named eight new members to a key advisory panel that shapes which preventive health services millions of Americans can get for free.

Kennedy’s picks for the 16-member U.S. Preventive Services Task Force — which has met only once since he took office — include a pediatric oncologist, two cardiologists and a radiologist, in a shift from previous administrations who have largely appointed only general practitioners.

Instead of having three co-chairs, the task force will be chaired solely by Seth Corey, a pediatric hematologist-oncologist at Cleveland Clinic.

The seven other appointees are Florida pediatrician Patrick Hunter, cardiologists Ronald Karlsberg and Venkatesh Murthy, family doctor Goldie Stands-Over-Bull, internist Louis Wilson, radiologist Dennis Wulfeck and healthcare delivery researcher Stephen Parente.

Hunter voted to restrict children from receiving gender transition care such as puberty blockers and surgeries when he served on the Florida Board of Medicine in 2022.

The task force is one of several groups of outside advisers to the Department of Health and Human Services that Kennedy has sought to reshape. He has taken a more active approach than previous health secretaries in selecting advisers he views as likely to advance his priorities on vaccines, autism research and preventive health.

“Prevention is one of our most powerful tools for confronting chronic disease,” Kennedy said in a statement. “We are strengthening the task force to ensure it asks hard questions, follows the evidence wherever it leads, and maintains the highest standards of scientific integrity.”

Primary care doctors have generally been considered most appropriate for the task force, which plays a major role in determining how easily people can access screenings for cancer and other illnesses. The panel issues recommendations and grades them based on the level of confidence in their net health benefit.

State Medicaid expansion programs and most private insurers must cover services graded “A” or “B” without charging patients any copays or deductibles. Recommendations with these high grades include mammograms, colonoscopies, pap tests and screenings for a range of other conditions.

Last year Kennedy upended the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which issues vaccine recommendations to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That panel has been suspended since March, when a judge ruled some of Kennedy’s 13 appointees to it weren’t sufficiently qualified.

In the case of the USPSTF, members rolled off naturally over the last year and a half as their terms expired. The eight new members announced Thursday join eight existing members.

The Washington Sun previously reported the administration was considering appointing Mark Shirley, whose daughter Malia Shirley works at HHS and is involved in the appointment process.

Former vice-chairs John Wong and Esa Davis, who the administration abruptly fired in May, had reapplied for their positions but neither were among the new members named Thursday.

As vice-chairs, Wong and Davis would normally have been involved in choosing new members to the group. Instead, the interviews were conducted only by staff within the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, which oversees the USPSTF.

entries.title: Trump Photos Suggest He’s Considering Plans to Demolish the Kennedy Center
entries.summary: The administration said in a filing that the Kennedy Center must be temporarily closed to “address significant safety hazards.”
entries.content:
New photos of President Donald Trump on Wednesday renewed fears that he plans to demolish the Kennedy Center as part of his bid to attach his name to the institution.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), who is fighting the closure in her role as an ex-officio board member, submitted the image on Thursday as part of her emergency plea to stop the venue from shutting down.

In the photos, which Brendan Smialowski of AFP shot outside Trump’s aircraft, the president is looking at a poster board that is partly obscured by the plane’s window. The photos show an aerial view of the building with a title above that reads “Kennedy Center” next to a partially covered word that appears to be “Demolish.”

The legal turmoil over whether Trump’s name can be inscribed to the venue, which a federal judge has repeatedly disallowed, has stirred speculation that the president may move to demolish the performing arts center entirely.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the poster board’s contents.

The Kennedy Center Board of Trustees voted on Wednesday to temporarily shutter the institution to allow for extensive renovations that are expected to cost $250 million.

However, Trump, who filled the board with allies who replaced previous members he dismissed last year, has stated that the construction would not begin unless his name is affixed to the building. The board has argued that the Kennedy Center is on the precipice of “financial collapse” and that recognizing Trump is vital to secure his fundraising prowess.

Trump told reporters on Wednesday that his administration should be recognized on the building.

“Because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close,” Trump said. “It will end up being ripped down.”

Beatty also included those remarks in her Thursday court filings.

The Justice Department subsequently asked Thursday for Beatty’s emergency hearing to be denied, saying the Kennedy Center must be temporarily closed to “address significant safety hazards,” according to court records.

The rebuttal referenced an incident earlier this month when a chunk of ceiling collapsed inside a main hallway following water damage from severe lightning storms that hit Washington.

“There is no emergency caused by Defendants’ temporary closure of the Center; the only emergency is the risk to the public and the Center’s employees and artists if it remained fully open without further safety assessment,” the Justice Department said.

Black fencing has been installed surrounding the Kennedy Center, and the building is closed to the public.

The Reach expansion campus next door continues to be open for programming, according to a Kennedy Center volunteer who spoke to The Washington Sun. But the volunteer said the center’s staff have received little information about what is happening.

“Nobody knows anything,” the volunteer said Thursday. “Staff is not being told anything.”

Security guards stationed outside the Kennedy Center said they were similarly in the dark. Asked about the board-approved renovations, one guard told The Sun he had “no idea” why the campus was closed.
