entries.title: Claims for Unemployment Benefits Drop
entries.summary: The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher gasoline prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began in February.
entries.content:
By Paul Wiseman

WASHINGTON (AP) — The number of people applying for unemployment benefits dropped sharply last week, another sign that layoffs remain rare and most Americans enjoy job security.

The Labor Department reported Thursday that jobless claims slid to 196,000, the fewest since mid-July and down from 206,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, dropped to 203,250.

Economists had expected claims to come in at 207,500, according to a survey by the data firm FactSet.

Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. For the past year, claims have mostly stayed within a historically low range of 200,000 to 230,000 a week.

The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher gasoline prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began Feb. 28.

Layoffs are low. Businesses, remembering the labor shortages that followed the end of pandemic lockdowns, are reluctant to let go of staff. They’re hiring — but modestly by the standards of recent years.

So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have been adding an average 80,000 jobs a month, including a surprising 162,000 in August. That is an improvement on a dismal 2025 when monthly job creation averaged 9,700 as high interest rates and President Donald Trump’s ever-changing trade policies discouraged hiring.

But it remains well below the 166,000 monthly jobs created, on average, in 2023 and 2024, and the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed COVID-19 lockdowns.

entries.title: U.N.-Backed Experts Say the U.S. May Have Committed War Crimes in Iran
entries.summary: They also accused Iran’s government of carrying out crimes against humanity.
entries.content:
By Jamey Keaten

GENEVA — Human rights experts commissioned by the U.N.’s top human rights body say they have found “reasonable grounds” to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab. They also accuse Iran’s theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people in a report published Thursday.

The report, while not binding, adds to international evidence gathered about crimes in the war in Iran, and could eventually be used in efforts to reach justice in international courts.

The fact-finding mission on Iran, chaired by jurist Sara Hossain of Bangladesh, is made up of independent experts and was created in 2022 by the Human Rights Council, the U.N.’s top human rights body, which is based in Geneva.

The experts were expected to present their findings on Monday to the council, which is made up of 47 U.N. member countries.

The Team Says the U.S. Launched ‘Indiscriminate’ Attacks

The international fact-finding mission says its findings on U.S. war crimes center on a pair of U.S. airstrikes that killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children.

At the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February, at least one U.S. missile hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, according to an Associated Press investigation. There has been no final accounting of what happened.

Iranian state media have said 168 people were killed in the strike, most of them children.

“Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects,” a U.N. statement about the team's findings said.

The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request from The Associated Press seeking comment.

In their report, the experts concluded that “the building of the school was the intended point of impact” and the resulting damage wasn’t the result of an errant strike or collateral damage from an attack on a compound of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard next to the school.

The Trump administration has yet to directly accept responsibility or release the findings of a Pentagon investigation into the school bombing.

The U.N.-backed team based its allegations on two strikes — one involving Tomahawk missiles that hit the “clearly identifiable” school, and another in which Precision Strike Missiles dispersed tungsten pellets over a “clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area” in the southern city of Lamerd, also on Feb. 28.

The U.N.-backed team said 22 civilian men and women were killed. U.S. Central Command has denied responsibility for the strike on Lamerd.

Experts Cite ‘Crimes Against Humanity’ by Iran's Government

The team found that killings by state security forces in Iran have occurred on a “staggering scale,” and civilians faced “gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government."

Iranian security forces carried out “violent repression” over the last two years by firing assault rifles into crowds, beating protesters and arresting healthcare workers, among other things, the team said. Detainees faced torture, and were deprived of legal counsel, leaving their families “in the dark” about their whereabouts, the experts said.

The Tehran government intensified the use of the death penalty, and said more than 70 people – including five women and three boys – remain at “imminent risk of execution,” they added.

“The report concluded that many of these gross violations amount to crimes against humanity — including murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians,” the statement said.

Both U.S. And Iran Should Provide Reparations, They Say

The experts said the United States and Iran should halt all rights violations and crimes, and provide “full reparations to victims.”

The report, built on a “victims-centered approach,” was based on interviews with 73 people both inside and outside Iran, along with documentation, satellite imagery, photographic and video material and information from “credible” organizations and experts, the experts wrote.

The ongoing conflict that has driven people from their homes in Iran as well as an internet shutdown and a lack of full cooperation from the two governments partially impeded the team's efforts to get information.

Nearly three dozen requests from the experts for information from Iran's government went unanswered, they said, as have requests in June to the U.S. government for information and meetings with officials.

entries.title: OpenAI Discloses 'Concerning' New AI Behavior
entries.summary: The announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including the leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns.
entries.content:
By Chan Ho-him

OpenAI has disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated.

The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including cases where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight.

OpenAI’s latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including the leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns.

Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots.”

In another instance, an AI “agent” used computer code to come up with the answer to a question, but, in order to have an online source to cite, it uploaded a file to the public internet without asking the user.

During training of an AI model called 5.6-sol, the model instructed itself to invent missing data, and an agent wrote a message to remind itself to hide mismatched information.

The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.

“As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research,” OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events.

“Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves,” the company said.

Wednesday’s new cases followed OpenAI’s disclosure in July that its rogue AI system hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing.

AI “agents” are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia.

That’s making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.

OpenAI's new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices.

“That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su added.

__

AP Business Writer Kelvin Chan in London contributed to this report.

entries.title: Republican Rep. Salazar Releases an Ad Criticizing Trump on Immigration
entries.summary: The Florida congresswoman called on Trump to think about the Hispanic voters who helped him win in 2024 who now feel “betrayed.”
entries.content:
Rep. María Elvira Salazar released an ad on Thursday directly criticizing some of President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts and calling on him to remember the Hispanic voters who propelled him to the White House in 2024.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” the Florida Republican, who is running for reelection in Florida’s 27th Congressional District, said in the 30-second spot. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.”

Salazar added that Trump needed to consider that “the same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” and compared what the president could do for the immigrant community to “what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism.”

Salazar is running against Democratic nominee Eliott Rodriguez, a former TV anchor, in the red-leaning district, which includes parts of Miami.

Salazar previously criticized Trump’s immigration rhetoric. She has advocated for maintaining Temporary Protected Status for some immigrant groups, including Venezuelans, and sponsored legislation to protect their status in the U.S. She has also attempted to force votes on legislation that would provide pathways to permanent citizenship for individuals with TPS and dreamers, undocumented individuals who were brought to the U.S. as children.

“I'm not talking about giving them amnesty. I'm talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land,” Salazar said in the ad, which is also running in Spanish.

In the ad, Salazar appeared to be in Lafayette Park in front of the White House, which is an area that has been fenced off from the public since January. The park has historically served as an area for protests, and Trump announced in June that the renovation to the park was almost complete.

Salazar cited July detention data in the ad, so it appears that it was filmed in the last few months.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: As Republican Cash Pours in for Paxton, Democrats Call for More Aid for Talarico
entries.summary: Democrats have been reluctant to invest in traditionally red Texas, but the polls show the party’s prospects are looking better in 2026.
entries.content:
Republicans are pouring in tens of millions of dollars to shore up the Senate campaign of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who has faced major struggles in his race against Democrat James Talarico. But Democrats are divided on whether to direct valuable resources to what’s been a solidly red state.

Some Democrats want their party to commit more money to aid Talarico on the expensive Texas airwaves. Republicans are outpacing Democrats in the spending race by more than $70 million this month, with Election Day fast approaching.

“I think we need to make sure that Talarico’s campaign gets the help it needs,” Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen told The Washington Sun this week.

A super PAC linked with Senate Republican leadership has spent more than $60 million in ads that will run this month, including a stunning drop of $54 million in a single day this week. President Donald Trump's super PAC threw in another $10 million, while Elon Musk's PAC is spending nearly $2 million for Paxton. There’s likely even more to come.

“I actually think Texas is worth investing in,” California Sen. Alex Padilla told The Sun.

Recent polls show a tight race in Texas, including an AARP poll where Talarico led Paxton 48% to 44% among likely Texas voters. A Siena Research/ReconMR poll released Thursday found Talarico with a slightly larger lead, 49% to Paxton’s 43%.

The flood of Republican cash is part of a larger effort by the party to save its congressional majorities in November. After some doubts about whether Trump’s political operation would open its wallet, and even with pleading by top GOP leaders, it has now reserved over $130 million to boost Republican candidates across several battleground states.

Talarico isn’t totally outgunned in the money race, however. His fundraising has set records in Texas this year, and he ended June with $21.5 million in the bank compared to Paxton’s $1.8 million. The disparity on the candidate side will likely only grow at the end of the third fundraising quarter next month.

But national Democrats haven’t committed significant resources in the race. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee announced a $40 million spend across 10 different Senate battleground states, including Texas, in July. Senate Majority PAC, the Democratic leadership aligned PAC, has not reported direct major spending investments in the race.

“Paxton is a weak, unimpressive candidate, and national Republicans coming in with millions to bail out his campaign only proves it,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC. “This is not a sign of strength for Trump or [Senate Majority Leader John] Thune, it’s a confirmation that nominating a scandal-plagued liability is indeed a liability. We are closely watching the state to ensure victory here.”

Senate Democrats believe they have the best chance of turning Texas blue in decades given Paxton’s ethical baggage, Trump’s low approval ratings and the sour political environment for Republicans this year. But they’re divided on how much to spend in a red state that has dashed their hopes before. And they know they’ll ultimately be outspent by well-funded Republican groups.

“Let me just say this about the money: They have the money, we have the people. I'll take the people any day,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told The Sun, touting the quality of Democratic Senate candidates in Texas and elsewhere in the country.

Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy said his party should “obviously” commit more resources in Texas, but he argued that Democratic candidates ought to use the Republican spending as an issue to campaign against money in politics.

“We’re not going to have as much money as they are. So the question is, how do we talk about the money with the limited resources we have?” Murphy said.

“Money is important, but it's not everything,” added Minnesota Sen. Tina Smith. “More money does not equal more votes, and what I think is happening around the country is people are fed up and kind of ignoring all of these TV ads.”

Another problem for Democrats is that resources are limited, and money is needed for candidates in other competitive battlegrounds. In Michigan, for example, Democratic Sens. Gary Peters and Elissa Slotkin asked their colleagues this week to help Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed with financial support. El-Sayed met with Democratic senators in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, after which the main Democratic Senate PAC committed an additional $10 million for Michigan.

In New Hampshire, top Democrats are ringing alarms about the campaign of Rep. Chris Pappas, who has lagged in some polls to Republican nominee and former GOP Sen. John Sununu.

Democrats are also eyeing pickup opportunities in other red-leaning states like Alaska, Ohio, North Carolina and Iowa, where Republicans are dropping large sums of money.

Republicans have their own money problems. Every dollar that they spend defending a seat in Texas is a dollar that isn’t going elsewhere, including trying to unseat vulnerable Democrats like Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia.

“At some point, I think you know, given scarce resources, they’re going to have to figure out where the money is going to do the most good, and it may or may not be a place like as big and as expensive as Texas,” Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn told The Sun this week.

Cornyn warned earlier this year that nominating Paxton would require Republicans to spend huge sums of money, and they could potentially lose his seat anyway, but Trump ignored him. The president endorsed Paxton, ousting the incumbent senator in a primary runoff.

Talarico has made fighting corporate and dark money in elections a core pillar of his Senate campaign. On the campaign trail, he frequently criticizes wealthy megadonors and billionaires for buying political influence. He dubbed last week’s Republican midterm convention in Dallas, where Trump raised money for Paxton, as a “Billionaire Ball” that ignored voters’ economic hardships.

Although national Republicans are spending large sums of money to bail out Paxton in Texas, they won’t get the same bang for their buck as Talarico’s campaign. Super PAC ads don’t receive TV discount rates that candidate ads do, per federal law, and are therefore much more expensive.

“Money does not change the fundamentals of the race,” said Luke Warford, the chair of the Democratic Party in Travis County, Texas, and the founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund, which raises money and provides structural support for Democratic candidates. “Super PAC money doesn’t go as far in terms of what you can buy on TV. It’s not as easy as just dropping a bunch of money.”

“Of course the Republican money is a challenge, but it also feeds into the narrative that Democrats are running against billionaires buying elections,” he added. “The money doesn’t come really without heavy baggage.”

Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said that ultimately, voters would make a judgment on the economy and high prices under Trump more so than any ads on television.

“Each of our candidates needs enough money to be able to respond [to Republican attacks],” she said. “But the real heart of this race is out there in plain view, without spending a nickel. Donald Trump's economy is not working for the American people, but Donald Trump's corruption is definitely working for Donald Trump.”

entries.title: Former Sen. Jon Kyl Dies at 84
entries.summary: The longtime Republican lawmaker shaped landmark water policies in the U.S. West and, as a lobbyist, guided the confirmation of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
entries.content:
PHOENIX (AP) — Former U.S. Sen. Jon Kyl, a longtime Republican lawmaker from Arizona who shaped landmark water policies in the U.S. West and guided the confirmation of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, has died. He was 84.

Kyl died Wednesday night from a neurological disorder, said Gordon James, a communications professional who is longtime friends with the Kyl family. Kyl had withdrawn from public life in December 2025 after announcing he had been diagnosed with dementia.

Kyl spent almost three decades in Congress, serving in both chambers, and watched his party undergo a drastic transformation, with his career spanning Ronald Reagan’s presidency to President Donald Trump’s first term.

Former Republican Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey, who considered Kyl a mentor, described the former senator in a February 2025 interview with The Associated Press as a true statesman and a “workhorse” among Washington, D.C.’s “showhorses.”

“If you saw him on the plane, he was sitting in the aisle, in coach, and he was reading,” Ducey said. “And he was reading potential bills or Senate business.”

Kyl rose to a leadership position during his last full term in the Senate, when his Republican colleagues selected him as minority whip. After retiring from politics in 2013 and becoming a lobbyist, Kyl returned to Congress briefly in 2018, when Ducey appointed him to fill the vacancy left by the late U.S. Sen. John McCain.

His appointment drew high praise from Trump, who said he was looking forward to working with “the extraordinary senator.” Kyl stayed for less than four months before rejoining lobbying firm Covington and Burling.

“At the federal level, and I regret to say that this is the case, but probably a lot of my better achievements were in preventing bad things from happening (rather) than forcing good things to happen,” Kyl said in a 2012 conversation with former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O’Connor.

Kyl was born in Oakland, Nebraska, on April 25, 1942, and grew up in a rural farming district in Iowa that his father represented in the U.S. House. At 18, he headed southwest to attend the University of Arizona, where he met his wife, Caryll, and earned a law degree.

Before being elected for the first of his four terms in the House in 1987, Kyl was a key participant in shaping Arizona’s 1980 groundwater code as a lawyer representing a large water utility. The first-of-its-kind code created a regulatory framework for managing groundwater in the drought-stricken state, largely centering on the state’s population centers, including Phoenix and Tucson.

In 2004, Kyl authored legislation that provided one of the largest tribal water rights settlements, which, after a decades-long battle, gave the Gila River Indian Community enough water to fill nearly 313,500 Olympic-sized swimming pools annually. Republican U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, who later served as majority leader, called Kyl's work ethic “legendary” in a 2012 floor speech and said Kyl had labored mostly behind the scenes for 15 years to advance the settlement.

“It was one of the hardest things I’ve ever done, but I was in a position to be the catalyst,” Kyl told the Phoenix New Times in a 2006 interview. “There wasn’t anybody else who could do that water deal. And it had to be done.”

Arizona State University’s Kyl Center for Water Policy takes its name from him. Its director, Sarah Porter, said Kyl was generous with his time and an effective member of the state’s congressional delegation who took a practical approach to water policy.

“He’s always sort of cared about the public good and been able to think about, ‘What will this mean for the generations to come?’” Porter said, adding that Kyl remained “quite a dynamo” until recent years, as his wife battled health problems.

Ducey said Kyl was a “giant” in the Senate, further describing him as serious, engaging, forthright and thoughtful. His biggest impacts, Ducey said, came from the way he kept the Republican caucus together in opposition to Obamacare and his staunch support of Israel.

Kyl also backed legislation to authorize construction of a fence stretching hundreds of miles along the U.S.-Mexico border. He later joined with Democrats to support a bill that would provide a path to citizenship and temporary guest-worker status for those in the U.S. without authorization. The proposal ultimately failed.

As a lobbyist, Kyl helped guide the confirmation of Trump-picked U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. When Kyl returned to the halls of Congress in 2018, he was known as Kavanaugh’s chief Sherpa — an informal but widely known term for a nominee’s guide to the political tundra in the Senate.

In a statement disclosing his dementia diagnosis, Kyl harkened back to the words of Reagan, when the former president revealed his own Alzheimer’s diagnosis and said he was starting a journey that would lead him to the end of his life.

Kyl said he shared Reagan’s confidence for Arizona and the nation’s future, and that despite his diagnosis, he was a “very fortunate man.”

entries.title: Park Service Says Trump’s Arch Should Proceed Despite Potential Harm to Historic Sites
entries.summary: The construction of the monument could affect sites including Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch will negatively affect nearby historic sites, but should be built anyway, according to the National Park Service.

In a new document circulated to local historic preservation groups, the agency said that, despite harm to the sites, the arch should move forward at its proposed location because that site is “central to the undertaking” of the project. The 250-foot monument is planned to be built near Arlington National Cemetery, inside D.C.’s border at Memorial Circle.

The arch’s “adverse effects cannot be fully avoided while retaining the location-dependent purpose” of the monument, the document said. Building it anywhere else would negate its intention to act as a “ceremonial gateway” in tandem with George Washington Memorial Parkway to celebrate “valor, sacrifice, and American heritage.”

The project, part of Trump’s campaign to reshape D.C., has faced legal pushback for its potential to obstruct the view of Arlington National Cemetery. In a report released last month, the National Park Service conceded that the monument is likely to disturb dozens of historic sites, including the cemetery, Arlington Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial.

In the new document, first obtained by The Washington Post, the park service said it would mitigate the arch’s impact by creating signs and webpages explaining the monument’s purpose to the public. The agency wants local historic preservation groups to sign the document, which is an agreement cementing the proposed mitigation, as part of a federally required feedback process.

If the preservation groups sign, it will probably expedite final approval for the arch, though the Trump administration does not need their approval to move forward.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in a statement this month that excavation work for the arch would start by Thursday, despite an ongoing court battle mandating prior notice of construction. As of Thursday, no ground has been moved at the site.

The National Park Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: The Nats Have Now Clinched a Seventh Straight Losing Season
entries.summary: Washington hasn’t had a winning campaign since its 2019 World Series title.
entries.content:
The Nationals reached a dubious milestone with Wednesday’s 3-0 loss to the Phillies, dropping to 71-82 and ensuring the team’s seventh consecutive losing season since winning the 2019 World Series.

Washington will enter the offseason with more reason for optimism than in years past, however. James Wood and CJ Abrams established themselves as players who could be pillars of the organization moving forward, with both earning All-Star selections this season and being no older than 25. The team’s farm system, which received a major overhaul prior to this season, has multiple top prospects, including Seaver King and Eli Willits, expected to be called up as soon as 2027.

But for as good as the Nationals’ offense has been — even after trading away infielders Luis Garcia Jr. (Yankees) and Curtis Mead (Red Sox) at the deadline — the team’s pitching has been a season-long issue. The bullpen has been on the wrong side of history, setting a major league record for blown saves with 39. In Wednesday’s loss, the team walked 13 batters, tying the Athletics for the most by any MLB team in a game this year.

And the finish does register as a disappointment in light of the team’s unexpectedly strong start to the season, having entered the All-Star break with a 48-49 record and in the mix for a wild card playoff berth.

The Nats do still have a chance to end the season on a high note. With nine games left, all against non-playoff teams, they need just one win to exceed their season total from any year since their title-winning campaign in 2019.

entries.title: Josh Shapiro Calls for Federal Government to Place ‘Strict Guardrails’ on AI
entries.summary: The governor and potential 2028 Democratic candidate sought a middle ground between being hands-off and seeking a moratorium on AI development.
entries.content:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro criticized Congress’ inaction on artificial intelligence regulation after industry leaders offered grim warnings of an AI revolt.

The governor, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, specifically criticized House Speaker Mike Johnson for what he described as abdicating “his responsibility to lead” after the House recessed until the November elections are over. That’s as artificial intelligence experts and CEOs have warned of the growing capabilities of the technology, which some industry experts have gone as far as to say is out of control.

“By the time Congress comes back into session after the election, we could be dealing with a whole new generation of generative AI with more scary examples of AI agents going rogue,” Shapiro said Thursday at the AI Horizons Pittsburgh Summit, a gathering of tech leaders and policy makers.

Shapiro said he is not a “doomer” and touted how his administration has incorporated AI — and fought against its abuses — in Pennsylvania.

Shapiro used his address to stake out a measured stance on artificial intelligence ahead of his possible 2028 bid. Other potential presidential contenders are scrambling to find their positions on AI after sobering calls this month from members of Congress and the industry itself to slow down the technology’s growth.

“The federal government needs to work with leading researchers and experts, as we've done here in Pennsylvania, and with the American people, not against them, to develop strict guardrails on this technology, its development, and its deployment in the real world,” he said.

President Donald Trump has been a champion of AI, arguing that the U.S. must keep a competitive edge on it. He said this week that “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT” is the only guardrail needed for the industry and wrote on Truth Social that “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.”

Shapiro countered: “It’s a false choice to say that our only two options in America are to do what Donald Trump is saying — that we should ignore the risks and go full steam ahead — or on the other hand, to completely stop work on AI development indefinitely.”

He called on Trump to make responsible regulation of AI a top issue in his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week while still recognizing the stakes of the global AI arms race.

“We need to beat China on AI,” the governor acknowledged.

The Washington Sun reported this week that Democrats considering a presidential run are looking for advice from the likes of Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), who supports a temporary pause on AI growth, and New York State Assembly member Alex Bores, who started an effort this week to help Democrats create a unified AI agenda after his failed congressional bid.

Shapiro once proposed incentives to bring data centers to cities like Pittsburgh, where he offered Thursday’s remarks, but has since changed course. In August, he signed an executive order to create “strict guardrails” for data center development, aimed at requiring data centers to receive community approval before building and commit to “strict environmental and transparency requirements.”

Pennsylvania, a crucial battleground state, currently has 100 proposed data centers, the state government says.

Many members of Congress are now on the campaign trail until November and will have to answer voters' concerns about AI, in addition to frustrations about rising gas and grocery prices. A poll shared with The Washington Sun found 60% of Americans believe the government should slow down AI development, even if that means letting China catch up. Potential presidential candidates are feeling that pressure too.

Shapiro is among Democrats having “productive conversations” with LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic donor Reid Hoffman, who also co-founded an AI company, Politico reported. Hoffman also named California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore.

entries.title: RFK Jr. Headlines Anti-Vaccine Group’s Conference, Discusses Chemtrails
entries.summary: The health secretary told Children’s Health Defense that it has a “strong and steadfast friend at the White House” in President Donald Trump.
entries.content:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spoke to a room full of vaccine skeptics Thursday afternoon as though he was coming home.

“I think I know most of the people in this room,” he told dozens of attendees at a one-day conference in downtown D.C. put on by Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine group he chaired from 2015 to 2023.

Kennedy’s presence at the conference — which featured speakers railing against vaccines as a major threat to children — highlighted his close ties to the anti-vaccine movement even as he runs the government health agency that administers major federal insurance programs, regulates drugs and oversees public health.

Kennedy assured attendees that President Donald Trump, who recently signed an executive order aimed at amending the childhood vaccine schedule, is their ally.

“Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy said.

Kennedy spent the first part of his 75-minute address touting his efforts to address chronic illness. But he quickly pivoted to more fringe topics, receiving spirited applause from the crowd as he vowed to probe for answers to their longstanding skepticism of vaccines, chemtrails and electric and magnetic fields.

Kennedy ticked through a list of vaccine-related initiatives at Health and Human Services, touting new research into the causes of autism, changes to childhood shots and efforts to change how adverse vaccine effects are reported.

But at one point, he seemed apologetic that HHS hadn’t achieved more changes in the 19 months he has served as secretary.

“A lot of people in this community … expected me to come in and upset this whole system,” Kennedy said. “We are doing this one day at a time.”

Kennedy stayed more disciplined in his criticisms of vaccines than other speakers at the conference. Before Kennedy spoke, the crowd heard from Mark Gorton, president of the MAHA Institute, a thank tank aligned with Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement.

In a presentation that included multiple charts and graphs, Gorton argued that giving children vaccines — which he called “nightmares” — has caused the worst-ever health crisis in the United States.

“Vaccine injuries are the largest scandal in the history of medicine,” Gorton said.

entries.title: U.S. Approves Visas for Iranian Leaders to Attend U.N. Meetings in New York
entries.summary: The State Department said "the core delegation from the Iranian regime" will be allowed to come to the U.S.
entries.content:
By Matthew Lee

The Trump administration has approved visas for top Iranian officials, including the president and foreign minister, to attend next week’s U.N. General Assembly high-level meeting in New York even as the two countries are locked in a stalemated war.

The State Department said Thursday that it had approved visas for Iran’s “core delegation,” along with essential staffers to participate in the U.N. meetings. The core delegation includes President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to visa privacy laws.

“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level week. The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year,” the statement said.

The move is unusual due to the more than six-month-long conflict between Iran and the United States and no sign that agreements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to talks on Iran’s nuclear program are close. It also comes as Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have stepped up attacks on Saudi infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, another major maritime route in the region where impediments have helped drive a surge in global oil prices.

In addition, Iran remains the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism, according to the United States, which has imposed significant sanctions against the country and launched a new campaign in recent weeks aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines."

As the host country for the United Nations headquarters, the U.S. is generally limited in what it can do to prevent foreign leaders from coming to the General Assembly. However, it has in the past denied visas to — or discouraged applications from — leaders involved in active conflicts with the United States.

For last year's U.N. meetings of world leaders — which took place before the Iran war began on Feb. 28 but after the U.S. and Israel launched air strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025 — the State Department also approved a limited number of visas for Iranian diplomats but also imposed rigid restrictions on the delegation's movements.

Those included severe limitations on how far Iranian officials could travel in New York City from their U.N. mission and barred them from shopping at wholesale membership stores, such as Costco and Sam's Club.

The decision on the Iranian visas was announced just a day after the State Department denied visas to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and his delegation to come to the General Assembly.

“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level week," the State Department said. "The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year.”

The department accused the Palestinian Authority — which administers parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank — of trying to “internationalize” the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza by bringing cases to the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court as well as continuing to pay stipends to prisoners jailed in Israel for attacks on Israelis.

The Palestinian Authority condemned the move and called Israel’s actions “the real threat to the two-state solution and prospects for peace.” It also said it remained committed to long-stalled negotiations but defended its efforts to gain Palestinian recognition through international bodies and courts.

“Punitive measures and restrictions imposed on Palestinian officials do not contribute to advancing peace or combating violence,” the authority’s foreign ministry said in a statement. “Rather, they weaken the Palestinian partner committed to a political solution and encourage forces working to undermine the two-state solution and impose the reality of occupation, settlement and annexation by force."

The U.S. does not recognize the Palestinian Authority as a full member of the United Nations, although the General Assembly and certain U.N. agencies and bodies have done so.

Associated Press writer Sam Metz in Jerusalem contributed to this report.

entries.title: Senate Stalls Major Data Center Bill That Sailed Through House
entries.summary: Senate Democrats blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act as insufficient, stalling the only AI-related measure that could pass this fall.
entries.content:
A day after the first major bill designed to curb the costs associated with data centers and artificial intelligence passed the House with flying colors, the legislation hit a wall in the Senate on Thursday.

The bill, the Ratepayer Protection Act, requires states to consider — but does not mandate — standards that would require AI data centers to pay the full cost of infrastructure upgrades to their facilities, instead of passing those costs on to consumers.

Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who sponsored the bill and is in a tough reelection race in a state where data centers are a hot issue, tried to pass the measure through unanimous consent to bypass the Senate’s lengthy legislative process. The procedure requires the agreement of all 100 senators.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico) objected, arguing the bill is just a recommendation that doesn’t sufficiently protect Americans from the costs of the booming industry. The blockade makes it all but certain an AI-related bill will not pass Congressbefore the midterms, even as the issue continues to be a focal point of anger across the country.

“The Ratepayer Protection Act falls short of what we need to do to respond,” Heinrich said while objecting to the bill on the Senate floor. “Rather than voluntary pledges or suggestions to states, Congress needs to pass real legislation with real teeth.”

Husted blasted Democrats for striking the bill down, writing on X that “Senate Democrats want Big Tech to get a free pass while your electric bill goes up.”

“Before we leave here, we ought to do something on a matter that the American people have asked us to do something about,” Husted said on the Senate floor. “It is a shame that this opportunity has been missed today, but I will be back to push this issue forward.”

Other Democrats also criticized the bill as not going far enough.

“We have to make sure we have something with enforcement,” Sen. Gary Peters (D-Michigan) told The Washington Sun. “I think we all agree that they should cover the cost, but we got to make sure they actually do that. Otherwise, it's just a hollow bill.”

Husted is defending his seat in a race the Cook Political Report has deemed a toss-up. Former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, Husted’s challenger, has made the costs of the facilities a major point in his campaign, running TV ads labeling Husted “the face of data centers.”

Some Democrats said they saw the move to advance the bill as a political maneuver to help Husted.

“Data centers is a key issue, and Jon Husted is in a very tough race for election to the United States Senate,” said Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois), the chamber’s minority whip. “This is a frequent approach, last-minute legislation on a subject that is controversial.”

Though most House Democrats backed the measure, Senate Democrats pointed to a number of other bills that have been introduced in the upper chamber that could more forcefully regulate costs stemming from data centers.

Heinrich pointed to his own bill, the GRID Savings Act, which would require large users of electricity to abide by rules similar to those for power plants and would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to establish new rules around data centers’ electricity usage. He sought consent to pass his bill, but Republicans objected.

entries.title: ‘I Support My Country,’ Alex Ovechkin Says After Pro-Putin Appearance
entries.summary: Ovechkin, who took part in a campaign ad for United Russia earlier this month, called for “peace and love.”
entries.content:
Alex Ovechkin began his first Capitals media availability of the season by addressing his recent appearance in a United Russia video supporting President Vladimir Putin.

“I’m Russian,” Ovechkin said. “As soon as I’m done playing hockey, I’m probably going to stay there. I’m going to live there. My kids are going to live there, my family. I’m full of peace and love, and I hope everything’s going to be OK. My home is Russia. D.C. is my second home. … I hope everything’s going to be OK. Peace and love for everybody.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

The Capitals released a statement earlier this week saying that Ovechkin “was asked by his country” to appear in the video, which also featured Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov. Asked on Thursday for more detail, Ovechkin said, “They asked me to do that, so I said yes. As simple as that.” He was then asked why he participated in the campaign.

“I’m Russian, and I support my country,” Ovechkin said. “I’m for peace and love, I hope, in the world. It doesn’t matter who you are. I hope everybody understands that everybody wants peace, and I hope everything is going to be OK in the world.”

He then smiled and changed the subject.

“Let’s do hockey questions.”

With Russian parliamentary elections taking place this weekend, the video began circulating widely online Monday after it was shared by the Russian newspaper Vedomosti. In the ad, Ovechkin is pictured standing alongside more than two dozen Russian celebrities and government officials. The video sparked heated responses, including from Rep. Joe Wilson (R-South Carolina), who sent a letter to NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman.

“I write with serious concern regarding the recent appearance by Washington Capitals Captain Alexander Ovechkin (#8) in a political campaign advertisement for United Russia, the dictatorial political party of Russian war criminal Vladimir Putin, who actively works to oppress the people of Russia by outlawing freedom of speech and fair elections,” wrote Wilson, who is on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

“The advertisement comes ahead of Russia’s September parliamentary ‘elections’ and represents an alarming instance of one of the National Hockey League’s most prominent players lending his image and international celebrity to a political organization that has enabled Putin’s brutal rule and his ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine,” Wilson wrote.

Ovechkin has long had a public relationship with Putin. In 2017, he started a social media campaign to support the politician called “Putin Team,” and his Instagram profile picture shows him with Putin. Ovechkin was born in Moscow and traditionally spends his offseasons in Russia.

"I would say it's a difficult situation, and I understand why people are upset," Capitals general manager Chris Patrick said on Thursday. "And that's probably the most I should say about it as a general manager of a hockey team, and not someone well-versed in geopolitical issues."

Patrick was later asked for his thoughts on the position Ovechkin is in.

"I mean, I feel bad for him," the executive said. "It may not be a popular sentiment among people critiquing him right now, but it's a hard situation for him."

This is Ovechkin’s 22nd season with the Capitals. The NHL’s all-time leading scorer, who turned 41 on Thursday, decided against retirement this summer and signed a one-year, $4.25-million contract to return to the team.

“I haven’t seen the video, but I know this: [He] has done an amazing job in my time here. I love him, I love his family, and he’s a big part of our team,” Capitals coach Spencer Carbery said. “Him being our captain, the relationship I have with him as a coach here, it doesn't affect that.”

entries.title: Neighbors Upset Over Federal Agents’ Presence at D.C. School
entries.summary: Agents and National Guard troops handed out fliers outside a Northwest elementary school, as a helicopter hovered overhead.
entries.content:
Dozens of federal agents accompanied by National Guard troops fanned out around an elementary school in Northwest D.C. on Thursday, prompting questions and concerns from some residents while also serving as a vivid reminder of the Trump administration’s continuing and aggressive public safety efforts in the city.

The unexpected yet highly visible deployment — which included a U.S. Park Police helicopter hovering low over the neighborhood — started earlier this morning as students were filtering into Bruce-Monroe Elementary School in Park View.

“We heard a helicopter circling overhead really low,” said one parent who was in the school at the time. “Staff started to ask what was going on, and then some of the group chats in the neighborhood started posting that there’s a National Guard and FBI presence.”
Park Police helicopter (3024x4032, AR: 0.75)Parents and neighbors came out to observe, and say they saw groups of National Guard troops accompanying federal agents — including from the FBI, U.S. Marshals Service and Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency (CSOSA) — as they walked around the vicinity of the school and fanned out on nearby streets.

“Some parents asked them what they were doing, they said they were being a friendly face and keeping the neighborhood safe and beautiful,” said the parent, who spoke to The Washington Sun on the condition of anonymity.

Chad, who declined to give his last name, said the agents were also handing out fliers offering cash rewards for tips leading to convictions for specific crimes — from $2,500 for illegal guns to $50,000 for murders. (D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department separately offers its own rewards for tips.)

Brady McCarron, a spokesman for the U.S. Marshals Service, told The Sun that the agents and troops were in Park View as part of a new effort launched by the D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force. The task force is a federal entity created to coordinate law enforcement efforts in the wake of President Donald Trump’s decision in August 2025 to surge federal agents into the city and deploy the National Guard.

“Each time one of those areas is chosen, it is because there is either a high amount of calls for service, or a high amount of warrants, or an amount of CSOSA checks that need to be performed,” said McCarron.

There was a spate of shootings in Park View in early August — including one that left visible bullet holes close to the school and a nearby recreation center. A similar show of federal force was reported in Brookland earlier this summer.

The presence of federal agents in D.C. has ebbed and flowed over the last year. Initially ICE was more active in D.C. neighborhoods, later replaced by officers from Homeland Security Investigations patrolling alongside MPD. Mayor Muriel Bowser has allowed MPD to work with the federal task force, arguing that having local officers along would better focus federal efforts on violent crime.

In this case, though, MPD spokesman Darran Todd said local officers were not involved. “MPD was made aware of a federal agency presence near an elementary school. MPD members were not involved and were not present on scene,” he wrote in an email.

The National Guard’s presence ramped up over the summer, with more troops seen patrolling the city’s neighborhoods. It has since decreased; there are now just over 3,100 troops in the city, down from almost 5,000 earlier in the summer. Still, the National Guard is expected to maintain its presence in D.C. through 2029.

Park Police has increased its local enforcement efforts in D.C., making more arrests and engaging in high-speed police chases — some of which have ended with injuries and fatalities.
Park View troops (1536x2048, AR: 0.75)Trump and other federal officials say their efforts have contributed to the decline in crime in D.C. As of this week, homicides are down 30% compared to the same period last year — but overall violent crime is up 8% due to a significant uptick in assaults with dangerous weapons. Critics say crime was decreasing before Trump surged resources into the city, and that federal agents and National Guard troops have antagonized local communities.

“It is scary for my kids to see armed soldiers walking around in large groups with the FBI circling their school and playground,” said the Park View parent who spoke to The Sun. “It makes it seem to them like something really scary is going on outside. As a parent I don’t want my kids to get used to armed guards patrolling the street.”

Last month, residents in Trinidad protested after the National Guard repeatedly staged in the parking lot of the neighborhood’s elementary school.

Chad similarly argued that the presence could be traumatizing for the neighborhood’s Latino population; 65% of the school’s 448 students are Latino. “They see these people and the vests and they think ICE. They are in a constant state of fear. So this is a problem,” he said.

Ward 1 Council member Brianne Nadeau visited the school after hearing of the federal presence, and later said in a statement that she had asked MPD to request that agents and troops not patrol in the school’s direct vicinity. She also said that parents and neighbors would be present outside as kids get out in the afternoon to ensure they can leave safely.

“As the National Guard, ICE, HSI, DEA, and other federal agencies patrol our streets, our residents continue to live in fear. This is unacceptable,” she said in a statement. “Our kids and their families should be able to go to school without feeling intimidated and scared of armed guards lining the sidewalks. Our schools should be welcoming environments for our students, just as our District should welcome all who wish to call it home.”

Nadeau also called on the police chief to rescind the decision to let local officers work with federal agents.

“It’s time for federal agents to leave our communities alone,” she said in the statement.

Ward 4 Council member Janeese Lewis George, the Democratic nominee for mayor, has pledged to limit cooperation with federal law enforcement on the first day of her term in January.

entries.title: Trump Withdraws His ICE Nominee After Pushback
entries.summary: Department of Homeland Security officials reportedly questioned Lance Schroyer’s qualifications to lead the federal agency.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump withdrew his nominee for the head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to a notice posted to the White House’s website, after his pick faced skepticism from lawmakers and agency insiders.

Trump had nominated former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer, a former U.S. Marine with close to three decades of law enforcement experience, to replace former ICE acting Director Todd Lyons. Lyons, who resigned in April, was a key figure in carrying out the Trump administration’s mass deportation efforts and ICE raids across the country.

Although Schroyer also had support from Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former Oklahoma senator with a personal connection to Schroyer, some DHS officials questioned his lack of experience in managing large law enforcement agencies, according to Politico.

The Wall Street Journal reported in August that Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky), the chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, was stalling Schroyer’s nomination until he received more information on the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration agents this year in Minneapolis.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on why it withdrew Schroyer’s nomination.

Mullin, who appointed Schroyer as one of his senior advisers, defended Schroyer’s nomination in an August interview with Fox News, saying the Trump administration wanted someone who could be easily confirmed by the Senate.

The Senate has not confirmed an ICE director since Sarah Saldaña’s three-year tenure during the Obama administration. The agency has been led by acting directors since then.

entries.title: Man Sentenced to 14 Months for Attacking Ilhan Omar
entries.summary: The 56-year-old sprayed vinegar at the Democratic congresswoman during a town hall.
entries.content:
By Tim Sullivan

MINNEAPOLIS — The man who sprayed vinegar at Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar during a Minneapolis town hall was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison after reaching a deal with prosecutors.

The sentencing of 56-year-old Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the Jan. 27 assault. At the time, Minneapolis-St. Paul was facing an immigration crackdown that led to angry protests, arrests and the killing of two U.S. citizens by federal officers.

Kazmierczak was also sentenced to three years of supervised release, which includes no contact with Omar. U.S. marshals escorted him from the courtroom after he was sentenced.

“This wasn't a spur of the moment act,” U.S. District Judge Joan N. Ericksen said before handing down the sentence, noting that Kazmierczak had secured tickets for the town hall weeks in advance.

“An attack on a public figure is not a political statement. It is misguided, selfish, and inconsistent with any concept of a free or democratic society,” Ericksen said. Spraying anything at an elected official “is a terrifying thing, and you knew that when you did it.”

Omar's Attacker Apologizes for What He Did

Kazmierczak, who has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, shook visibly at times as he sat at the defense table. He spoke quietly and haltingly, occasionally wiping away tears as he stood before Ericksen.

He spoke about being a good neighbor, and how his troubles with insurance companies as well as prison had exacerbated his ailments. His attorney, John Fossum, argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medications before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened.

“I've spent enough time in jail thinking,” Kazmierczak said, his voice barely audible. “I really apologize to her for having put her through that,” he said, referring to Omar.

In an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak was unable to explain his actions, saying only “it's fuzzy” when Ericksen asked what he remembered.

“I’m sorry if I scared you,” he wrote to Omar after the attack.

Prosecutors Cite Evidence of Advance Planning

During the town hall, witnesses saw Kazmierczak jump up from the audience, spraying liquid from a syringe at Omar and saying she was “splitting Minnesota apart.” Omar’s security officers tackled Kazmierczak and turned him over to police, who arrested him.

Omar was not injured and continued with the town hall after the arrest.

Authorities later determined he had sprayed her with a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a U.S. officer.

The government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating he planned to do something at the meeting involving Omar “but would not answer their questions about his intent.”

He also sent messages to a neighbor to arrange for dog care and asking for bail bond company contact information.

The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse, had “a history of mental and emotional health concerns” and a string of health issues tied to his 2022 Parkinson’s disease diagnosis.

Omar, a refugee from Somalia, has long been a target of President Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant rhetoric. In 2019, after Omar’s election to Congress, Trump said she should “go back” to her country of birth. He has described her as “garbage” and said she should be investigated.

In social media posts, Kazmierczak had criticized former President Joe Biden and referred to Democrats as “angry and liars.” He wrote that Trump wants the U.S. to be “stronger and more prosperous.”

His attack came as the Minneapolis area was on edge due to the crackdown, with protesters often facing off against convoys of immigration officers and conservatives criticizing protesters.

entries.title: Texas Democrat Sees a Fundraising Surge Following Opponent’s Racist Posts
entries.summary: The candidate’s financial windfall follows Bo French’s viral post targeting South Asian students at a University of Texas-Austin football game.
entries.content:
Republican Bo French’s racist social media posts targeting South Asian university students have resulted in a fundraising windfall for his Democratic opponent in Texas’ railroad commission race.

State Rep. Jon Rosenthal told The Washington Sun on Thursday that he’s raised around $150,000 — major dollars for a Democrat in what is normally an under-the-radar race — after French posted a photo of a crowd of South Asian students at the University of Texas-Austin football game celebrating the school’s comeback win Saturday, saying, “the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

The comment drew national attention to the race. Rosenthal said his phone began “ringing off the hook” Sunday morning after the posts went viral and brought in a slate of new donors for him.

“For me, that’s monumental,” Rosenthal said. “It’s good to have the resources for the campaign, but certainly it’s even better to have the moral support and feel like people are with me.”

The Railroad Commission of Texas is a crucial regulatory agency: Commissioners, who are elected statewide for staggered six-year terms, no longer directly oversee the state’s railroads but rather its powerful oil, natural gas and utilities industries. A Democrat hasn’t served on the panel since 1999.

Rosenthal said the new influx of money will allow him to travel more throughout Texas in hopes of flipping people who supported French’s primary runoff opponent, Jim Wright, who lost by 14,800 votes in May, or less than one percentage point. The state representative also hopes to put spots up on AM radio and increase digital advertising across new counties.

“There’s no avoiding that this will be, in some part, a referendum on Bo French and his brand of politics,” Rosenthal said. “It does make this an opportunity to change the direction of politics in the state — and maybe even in the country.”

Rosenthal said that the donations he’s received since the remarks average $50. Campaign disclosures verifying the amounts he shared with The Sun aren’t due until October.

French did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Part of what’s made the backlash to French’s post so stunning is how many of the state’s most prominent GOP voices distanced themselves — particularly as the Republicans in the state are fighting to keep a Texas Senate seat and are seeing a drop-off in support among Latinos and other voters of color, despite stronger turnout among those communities over the last few election cycles.

Sen. John Cornyn told The Washington Examiner on Thursday that he would not vote for the Republican candidate, calling French an "embarrassment" to the party who would “drag the whole ticket down because of his racist comments.” And Karl Rove, a former George W. Bush adviser and longtime Republican political consultant, said he was going to vote for Rosenthal this week — his second time ever voting for a Democrat.

Rosenthal joked that he did not have winning Rove's support on his “bingo card” for the year.

Sabinal Mayor Erik Gomez, a Republican, said on Wednesday that he doesn’t know how to tell constituents in his majority-Hispanic region that they are welcome in the party.

“No Latino is going to see his comments and feel he resonates with them,” Gomez told The Sun in an email, saying he would still encourage fellow Republicans to vote within their own conservative views.

Despite losing the public support of several prominent politicians, French’s posts may not have turned off much of his base. This includes Republicans of color.

Ramesh Cherivirala, one of the founders of the Indo-American Conservatives of Texas, told The Sun that while members of his community were upset, many are still planning to vote for Republican candidates, including French, “in spite of his comments.”

But he still criticized the rhetoric French posted over the weekend.

“Most of the people I can think of in that arena, 99% of those kids — whether they are Pakistanis or Indians or any other race, Mexicans — they are born and raised here,” he said of the fans at the game. “He has absolutely no reason to say what he said.”

entries.title: Congress Hears an Apocalyptic Prediction From the ‘Godfather of AI’
entries.summary: Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton told lawmakers they have “maybe a year” left to regulate AI before its development spirals out of control.
entries.content:
The man known as the “Godfather of AI” issued an urgent warning to lawmakers this week that they only have a year or two left to regulate artificial intelligence before its development spirals out of control.

The prediction comes as pressure mounts for the government to institute guardrails on the industry, spurred by warnings from researchers and industry executives currently working on the technology.

Geoffrey Hinton, a computer scientist and cognitive psychologist who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in physics, told members of Congress in a closed-door briefing that they have “maybe a year, but not much more than a year,” according to an NBC News summary of the meeting published Thursday.

“If you look at predictions for when we’ll get superintelligence,” Hinton said, “it used to be maybe 30 years, maybe 50 years. Then it came down to maybe 10 years, maybe 20 years. Now people are saying, a lot of the researchers are saying only a few years.”

Hinton quit his job at Google in 2023 so he could speak freely about the risks of AI. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) invited Hinton and other experts in the field to Capitol Hill for a bipartisan briefing for lawmakers about the dangers of the rapid pace of development in the industry — though Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) was the only Republican to attend.

"Interesting speakers. I had a bill on the floor, I had to leave, but I enjoyed it," Kennedy told The Washington Sun. Still, he isn’t optimistic that the briefing will spur any action in the Senate.

"Quite frankly, if the reporting in The Wall Street Journal I read this morning and elsewhere is accurate, Secretary Bessent is pushing the White House to come up with some sort of framework to ensure the safety of the models,” Kennedy said. “That’s the next step I expect to happen. Is anything going to happen over here in the Senate? I don’t see any indication."

It was an assessment shared by Sen. Rick Scott (R-Florida), who said in an interview on NewsNation Thursday that the odds of Senate action on the issue were slim.

“With regard to destroying mankind, these companies need to do the right thing on their own. We’re not going to get smart enough to regulate them,” Scott said. “We’re not going to get something done up here.”

Some Democratic lawmakers, however, called for immediate action after listening to Hinton at the briefing.

“[Hinton] was very clear: AI technology has reached a point where it’s building itself. It can and will continue to go beyond human control - and therefore - our window to regulate it is disappearing rapidly. We must pause NOW,” Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Arizona) wrote Thursday on X.

Ansari wrote a letter Thursday with dozens of her colleagues demanding that President Donald Trump take action on AI immediately and called on the U.S. to work with international competitors like China to “to avert potentially devastating consequences.”

Trump has largely brushed off concerns about AI spiraling out of human control, saying that his presidency is the only necessary guardrail and calling the public fear a “hoax.”

“I am the Hoax Buster, and I’m right now breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!” Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social.

Trump has also repeatedly said “whoever wins, AI wins,” to argue against cooperation with China on AI development.

entries.title: Federal Judges in Minnesota Speak Out Against Trump’s DOJ in Rare Interviews
entries.summary: Judges told The New York Times they presided over bloated dockets and were subjected to a flood of death threats during ICE’s January operations.
entries.content:
Court officials faced near-constant threats of violence amid a surge of immigration raids that brought Minnesota's court system to its knees during the Trump administration’s crackdown earlier this winter, judges said in a series of interviews published Thursday.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in January arrested thousands of individuals and killed two U.S. citizens during Operation Metro Surge. The crackdown overwhelmed the Twin Cities and flooded Minnesota’s federal courts with civil lawsuits and emergency petitions filed to challenge unlawful ICE detentions.

Months later, seven of those judges — including Patrick Schiltz, who served as chief judge of the U.S. District Court for Minnesota through June — agreed to give interviews to The New York Times, an unusual occurrence for a group tasked with maintaining an impartial legal system.

Caseloads doubled overnight, judges described, while habeas corpus petitions grew a hundredfold. In January alone, ICE violated nearly 100 court orders from federal judges in the state. The pileup in Minnesota’s federal court system, Schiltz told the Times, “created a grave threat to the rule of law.”

Judges frequently had to reference agents’ noncompliance with the law in court documents. While the failure to follow legal procedure was primarily due to “incompetence and staffing shortage,” Schiltz told the newspaper, he expressed real concern that the Justice Department was not taking the court’s concerns seriously.

“ICE is not a law unto itself,” Schiltz, a George W. Bush appointee, wrote in a January court order.

“Due process is not a game of keep-away,” another judge, Nancy E. Brasel, said in a ruling mandating rights for detainees.

Before long, the district court’s efforts to maintain the rule of law in Minnesota became the subject of fierce scrutiny from conservative media commentators.

The attention drummed up “a deluge” of violent threats against the judges, according to the Times article. Court clerks fielded hundreds of calls and emails each day — some vowing to “kill u soon.”

On one occasion, after Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon maligned Judge Douglas Micko in a media appearance, Schiltz said that Micko and his family had to be “moved to a secure location” for several days due to serious threats on the judge’s life, the Times reported, adding that the administration’s comments were partly responsible for putting Micko in danger.

Judges kept a constant watch on their cell phones and were constantly fearful they’d miss an urgent petition, according to the report, knowing a single missed request could have life-altering consequences for detainees.

A press release the DOJ released ahead of Metro Surge stated that ICE planned to target “the worst of the worst” flocking to Minnesota “because they know sanctuary politicians will protect them.”

Judge John R. Tunheim, a Clinton appointee, told the Times “They weren’t arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street.”

In the seven months since the operation ended — during which President Donald Trump fired Kristi Noem from her post as homeland security secretary — the judges have put most of the cases related to Metro Surge behind them.

In that time, Schiltz has taken “senior status,” an early form of retirement. His retirement has given him the opportunity to reflect on the court’s hostile run-in with the DOJ in January, as the department attempted to sidestep the bench’s legal authority.

“The rule of law to democracy is like oxygen to a human body,” Schiltz said. “It is something that you absolutely need to survive, and yet it’s something that people just take for granted.”

entries.title: Trump Says U.S. Is Making ‘Major Progress’ on Army Base in Poland
entries.summary: The European ally has pushed for a larger permanent American military presence for months.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Thursday that the United States is making “major progress” toward establishing a permanent Army base in Poland, a move that could expand American military presence on NATO’s eastern flank.

“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance.”

Polish President Karol Nawrocki welcomed Trump’s announcement and said his government would work to provide “the best possible location for the US Army base.”

The announcement comes a week after Pentagon officials traveled to Poland for talks on expanding the military’s presence there.

A U.S. delegation led by Pentagon official William Cappelletti met with Polish officials and visited sites in Powidz and Poznan. The two sides agreed to create working groups.

It is not clear whether either location is being considered for the proposed base.

The Army already has a permanent presence in Poland. U.S. Army Garrison Poland is headquartered in Poznan, and V Corps maintains a forward headquarters there.

But much of the larger U.S. force in Poland, about 10,000 service members, is rotational, with troops deploying there for limited periods rather than being permanently stationed. Trump announced in May that the U.S. would send another 5,000 troops to the country.

That rotational presence has already sparked tension this year. The Pentagon halted a planned rotation of roughly 4,000 Army soldiers to Poland in May, surprising Polish officials and drawing criticism from some lawmakers. Poland’s defense minister said in July that the rotation would resume.

That leaves a major question about what Trump’s proposed base would change. The administration has not said whether it would build a new installation, expand an existing site or permanently station additional Army units in Poland.

The Pentagon referred all questions to the White House, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Poland has pushed for a larger permanent American presence for months. The Polish government formally proposed a permanent U.S. base earlier this year and has begun preparations for negotiations over its location, infrastructure and cost.

Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said in June that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had responded positively to the proposal, though no final agreement had been reached. Kosiniak-Kamysz is set to meet with Hegseth again next week in Washington to discuss the matter along with Russia-related threats to NATO’s eastern flank and Poland’s security.

The talks are unfolding as the Pentagon reviews the broader U.S. military presence in Europe, including whether to reduce or reposition some of the roughly 80,000 American troops on the continent.

entries.title: Trump Administration Allows Inadvertent Killing of Endangered Species
entries.summary: Experts say it creates a loophole that allows companies to build or log, even if they are aware that doing so will harm wildlife.
entries.content:
BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — Inadvertently killing endangered animals while logging a forest or building a dam would no longer be considered illegal under a new interpretation of the Endangered Species Act by federal officials, marking a sea change by President Donald Trump’s administration in how the landmark environmental law is enforced.

A directive sent to U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service employees this week says imperiled animals or plants must be intentionally targeted for their killing to be considered illegal.

That's a sharp turnaround from past practice at the wildlife service, which historically held people liable even for accidentally harming protected species such as grizzly bears, manatees and spotted owls.

Experts said the change would allow timber companies to log forests in the Pacific Northwest even if they knew that doing so could kill imperiled birds in the trees, or for developers to build a dam knowing it would kill salmon.

“This cuts against the entire history of the Endangered Species Act,” said Dan Ashe, who led the Fish and Wildlife Service under former President Barack Obama.

“It just creates a huge loophole,” added Ashe, who is now president of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. “It completely relieves people of any responsibility for their actions, even consequences that can be easily predicted.”

Encouraged by Republican lawmakers and industry lobbyists, officials under Trump have moved to dismantle key parts of the endangered species law and make companies exempt from its regulations. Administration officials have said they are returning the law to its original intent, following a 2024 Supreme Court decision that limited the authority of federal agencies to interpret environmental statutes passed by Congress.

States and conservation groups have filed numerous lawsuits seeking to turn back the changes.

The new interpretation of what it means to harm — or “take” — a species was detailed in a Sept. 14 directive from Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik.

“Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them,” Nesvik wrote, adding that the bats would only be impacted “indirectly and accidentally.”

The directive, reported earlier by The New York Times, leans heavily on a dissenting opinion from former Justice Antonin Scalia in a 1995 Supreme Court case. It comes on the heels of a new rule from the wildlife service in July that narrowed the definition of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act, or ESA.

Nesvik's directive will guide how that new rule is put into action, according to a Thursday statement from the Interior Department, which includes the Fish and Wildlife Service.

“Under the guidance, the ESA’s prohibition on ‘take’ continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife,” Interior Department officials said.

For decades, the government had defined harm to imperiled animals broadly to include encroachments on places where they live. Environmentalists warn the recent moves, if allowed to stand, will speed extinctions by letting protected species be killed and opening the door to habitat destruction.

“This is basically a free for all,” said Noah Greenwald with the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental group. “It's a radical reinterpretation that would put polluters and other industry before the natural world.”

The Endangered Species Act is credited with bringing back iconic animals — including the bald eagle, American alligator and California condor — from the brink of extinction.

Republicans rolled back several provisions of the law in Trump’s first term, only to have those moves reversed under Democratic President Joe Biden, then revived yet again during Trump's second term.

entries.title: Curtains for the Kennedy Center?
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Sept. 17, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

New photos of Donald Trump published last night renewed fears that he plans to demolish the Kennedy Center as part of his bid to attach his name to the institution.

  • One photo, shot by AFP’s Brendan Smialowski, shows Trump looking at a poster board with the words “Kennedy Center” and a partially covered word that appears to be “Demolish.”
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ordered the center to provide a detailed update on its “temporary closure” by next Wednesday, asked for 30 days’ notice before any “demolition” of the main building, and allowed Rep. Joyce Beatty’s team to seek discovery to investigate the poster board Trump was viewing.

THE HILL

The Protect College Sports Act reached 77 votes of support today ahead of a likely final Senate vote next week.

  • One new amendment requires schools seeking a change in conference to have been independent for only three years, not five.
Rep. María Elvira Salazar released an ad — shot outside the White House — directly criticizing some of Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts and calling on him to remember the Hispanic voters who helped propel him into office in 2024.

  • The Florida Republican, who represents a Latino-majority district that encompasses Miami, has been a staunch supporter of TPS extensions and immigration reform.
Senate Democrats blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act as insufficient, stalling the House-approved measure — the only AI-adjacent bill that had a chance of passing this fall.

THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Republicans are pouring out millions to support Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who has faced major struggles in his race against James Talarico. But Democrats are divided on whether to direct valuable resources to the state representative in what’s been a solidly red state.

THE ADMINISTRATION

Trump withdrew Lance Schroyer’s nomination for the head of ICE after he faced skepticism from lawmakers and agency insiders.

RFK Jr. headlined an anti-vaccine group’s conference this afternoon, at one point pivoting to fringe topics like chemtrails or electric and magnetic fields.

  • The Health and Human Services secretary is reshaping another key public health task force after appointing eight new members. 
Trump floated establishing a U.S. Army base in Poland in collaboration with President Karol Nawrocki today on Truth Social.
